PUBLIC OPENING CEREMONY
Sunday, October 12, 1997
2:30 P.m.

The Public Opening of Grand Lodge was held in the Masonic Aud itorium
of the California Masonic Memorial Temple, 1111 California Street, San
Francisco, California.beginning at 2:30 p.m. Grand Lodge was raised by the adu lt
leaders of the Order of De Mo lay in California, Brother Edwin Clarke, Executive
Officerofthe Jurisdiction of Northern California, and Brother Gaylord V. Roten,
Executive Officer of the Jurisdiction of Southern Jurisdiction. The gavel and
sounding b lock were made from scrub oak by Worshipful Brother Fred L. Weiss,
and were presented to the Grand Master on July 11, 1997, on the occasion of his
visit to the Chico Masonic Family Center for a reception hosted by the 21 Th and
222'h Masonic Districts.
Grand Master Allen B. Gresham, accompanied by his Grand Lodge
Officers, entered the Auditorium to the sound of trumpets and organ, and assumed
their stat ions. The Grand Chaplain gave the invocation.
The Grand Master asked the Grand Marshal to retire and present the Flag
of Our Country, which was done. Those present j o ined the Grand Master in the
Pledge of Allegiance, after which the Flag was placed in its proper positio n in the
East.
A Pageant honoring the several branches of the military services and the
Flag of Our Country thrilled those in attendance. The pageant was arranged by
Brother {and Major General) Ronald Markarian, the Chainnan of the Un ited States
Constitution Observance Committee. The National Sojourners assisted h im in
present ing the program. The gro ups participating in the pageant were:
Duncan Polytechnical High School -- Air Force JROTC
Fresno High School -- Anny JROTC
Fresno High School Naval Sea Cadet Corps
Sanger High School -- Naval JROTC
Selma High School -- USMC JROTC
McLane High School -- Anny JROTC
National Sojourners -- Heroes of '76

The Grand Master then introduced Ms. Amy Bickert. a teacher who has
special insight into the Masonic Student Assistance Program. Ms. Bickert spoke
movingly about how she had been aided by a dedicated and devoted teacher who
had received the MSAP training in Pennsylvania. She enthusiastically supported
th e program and graciously thanked the Masons for their involvement and
dedication to students. The Grand Master thanked her for her inspiring remarks.
In accordance with the Grand Master' s theme ''Quality is the Key - You
Can Make a Difference," the Grand Master then introduced Brother Jerry Burk. a
member of Bakersfield Lodge No. 224. who shared his thoughts on this theme.
Brother )erry L. Burk moved to Bakersfield. California in 1962. where h e
completed high school and received an Associate of Arts degree from Bakersfield
Community College. He graduated from Fresno State University, and fol lowed
one of his professors to the University of Montana where he completed his Master
of Arts in 1968, and then to the University of Oklahoma where he received his
Doctorate in 1972.
He taught for ten years in various universities before moving to industry.
where he worked as a consultant for several major corporations. including Martin
Marietta and Sara Lee. In 1989 he returned to Bakersfield after a twenty-two year
hiatus and founded The Burk Group. his organization performance and
development consulting business.
He was raised to the Third Degree of Masonry in 1990. and is a member
of the Scottish Rite and of the Shrine. He and his wife Sharon will be Worthy
Matron and Worthy Patron of Bakersfield Chapter No. 125, Order of the Eastern
They have two sons, Jerry and Christopher. and one

DEVOTIONAL SERV ICE

The Grand Lodge Devotional Service was held at Grace Cathedral, across
the street from the California Mason ic Memorial Temple. At 5:00 p.m. the Grand
Master led the Grand Lodge Officers in procession to their assigned seats. Broth er
Edward Mahoney, Senior Warden of Silver Gate Lodge No. 296, a Sconish Piper,
led the procession of Grand Lodge Officers and guests to the Cathedral.
The Invocation was led by the Grand Chaplain, followed by welcoming
remarks by the Grand Master and Readings From the Sacred Texts by M: W :. R.
Stephen Doan, Past Grand Master (Appendix G). The Grand Chaplain delivered
the Message (Appendix G).
Music was provided by the Cathedral Organist, and by Wor. Mark Harris.
a Past Master of Oriental Lodge No. 144.

by the Grand Master, and adjourn ed to the Grand Master's Banquet at the Fainnon t

ANNUAL COMMUN I CAT ION

The 148'h Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand Master
Allen B. Gresham at 9:00 a.m. on Monday, October 13, 1997. The Grand Lodge
had been raised by the Worshipful Michael Betschart, Master; George M.
Georgiou, Senior Warden: and the Worshipful Jake Flood, PM, Secretary of San
Bernardino Lodge No. 178. The raising of Grand Lodge had been followed by the
entrance of the Grand Lodge Officers to Purcell' s Trumpet Voluntary in C, who
took their regular stations. Gavels used at the morning session were the follow ing:
I) the gavel that was presented to the Grand Master' s father when he was installed
as Master of El Centro Lodge No. 3 84 in 1949, and presented by the Grand Master
to his father at that time: 2) a gavel handcrafted by Wor. Glenn Johnson, PM ,
Secretary of San Dimas Lodge No. 428; and 3) the Raintree Cross Gavel
handcrafted of orangewood by Wor. Gordon Westervelt, a Past Master of
Riverside Lodge No. 635.
The Grand Secretary was asked to ca ll the roll of Grand Lodge Officers,
Past Grand Masters. and Past Grand Officers, and to ascertain if a constitutional

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Brother Louis Vincent Parell, a member of Tehama Lodge No. 3,
presented two inspirational vocal selections which were greatly enjoyed by those
present.
Most Worshipful Anthony P. Wordlow, kneeling at the altar, took his
obligation as Grand Master on the Historic Miner' s Bible. The historical
significance of this Bible was presented by Worshipful Brother Bruce Hart, a Past
Master of Tehama Lodge No. 3.
The Miner's Bible
This is the story of a Bible a very special Bible that, today, adorns the
altar of this Grand Lodge, a Bible that is the Rule and Guide of our Faith, a Bible
that is the Cornerstone of Freemasonry in California.
But, let me take you back ... back in history 150 years.
The origin of this beautiful Bible was lost in the great desert of Nevada.
The original owner. an unknown pioneer, abandoned this Bible along with other
books and household goods in a desperate attempt to lighten the load in his wagon,
that his animals, weakened by lack of water and scarcity of feed, might survive and
this early settler could continue in his struggle to reach the valleys of California.
Later, another weary traveler observed the discarded items by the trail,
stepped down off his wagon, and, for whatever reason, was attracted to this
handsome Bible which he picked up and placed by his side, where it rode, safe and
secure, as he continued his journey to the promise of California, the Land of Gold.
After a brief stay in Sacramento, this gold-seeker decided to pursue his
dream and try his luck in the mines and to lighten HIS load, gave the Bible to an
acquaintance, Dr. R. H. McDonald, who was known as a Mason. Later, in th e fall
of 1849, a Masonic Relief Association was formed in the City of Sacramento.
dedicated to the care of families in need. Dr. McDonald, hearing that this
association was in need of a Bible, presented this book, today known as the
MINER'S BIBLE.
During the early days of that Association, Brother Caleb Fenner presented
a charter from Hiram No. 1, A.F. & A.M ., of the State of Connecticut. In due time,
under the authority of this charter, the first Masonic Lodge was formed in
Sacramento known as.Connecticut No. 75. This Lodge was formed in January of
1850, and, on a crude Altar, the MINER' S BIBLE, in all its glory.
Later in the year of 1850. the Grand Lodge of California was formed. and,
again, the MINER'S BIBLE, was present. Subsequently, Connecticut No. 75
became Tehama Lodge No. 3, F. & A. M., one of the original Masonic Lodges in
California, and, in its possession. the MINER'S BIBLE, as it is today.

GRAND LOrx:JE OF CALIFORNIA

27

Over the years, the MINER'S BIBLE , has been present at many historic
events. Several early Governors chose to take their Oath of Office on this Bible.
In 1861 , at the Cornerstone Ceremonies for new California State Capitol, this Bible
was on the Altar, and it was present, again, in 1978, when the State Capitol was rededicated. And it was present HERE in 1950 when the Grand Lodge celebrated
100 years, and, again, in 1975 on the occasion of the I 25th anniversary of the Grand
Lodge of California.
During the solemn ceremonies of the Third Degree, every member of
Tehama No. 3 has rested his hands on this Bible and every memberofTehama No.
3 has his name entered on its pages and, today, the MINER'S BIBLE is, again,
present in this Grand Lodge, at rest on the Sacred Altar, as Anthony P. Wordlow,
a Past Master of Tehama No. 3, kneels, to take the obligation as Grand Master of
Masons for the State of California. Think abou·t the remarkable history of this
book. Hands on the Bible, linked with the past, and extended to the future, to
men yet unborn.
Following the newly-installed Grand Master's remarks, the Most
Worshipful Allen B. Gresham, Past Grand Master, was presented with his Past
Grand Master' s Apron, Jewel, and Wallet Card. Mrs. Clara Gresham was
presented with a bouquet of roses and a gift in appreciation for her time and
support of her husband and the Grand Lodge during his year as Grand Master.
The ceremonies were concluded with The Lord's Prayer, presented by the
Ben Ali Shrine Temple Chanters, from Sacramento, California. The Grand Lodge
Officers retired from the Auditorium to the accompaniment of the Ben Ali Pipes
and Drums, to attend the Gala Reception in the lobby of the California Masonic
Memorial Temple.
Closing of Grand Lodge
At 1:45 p .m., Deputy Grand Master Melville H. Nahin called Grand
Lodge from refreshmentto labor. Pursuant to the amendmentofSection.520 of the
California Masonic Code adopted at the Annual Com munication, the Grand
Secretary requested the Grand Master's approval to appoint Worshipful Joel H.
Springer III a.:. Assistant Grand Secretary. The Deputy Grand Master directed the
Grand Marshal to conduct Worshipful Brother Joel H. Springer III to a place in
front of the East, and proceeded to install him in the office of Assistant Grand
Secretary.
Grand Lodge was then closed in ample form.

'·The World Has Need of Masonry"
" Brethren, the world has need of Masonry. It needs our organized
support of free public education . It needs our love for, and adheres to, the
principles involved in the Constitut ion and the Bill of Rights. It needs our
steadfastness to the principle of the separation of church and state. It
needs our serious and solemn lessons of the brotherhood of a ll mankind
and the fatherhood of God.
Yes, Masonry itself is a vital necessity for the preservat ion of our
American democrat ic way of life, and every brother who has put his
shouldert o the wheel of this great Craft of ours this year, may enjoy the
inner satisfacti onofknow ing that he has helped to hold aloft the light of
Trust which will eventuall y penneate earth's darkest recesses and bring
to us the peace we seek. For the continued advancem ent of our beloved
fraternity. let us ever remembe r and always heed that admonitio n from the
Sennon on the Mount which seems to have been written especially for us.
' Ye are the light of this world ... Let your light to shine before men that
they ma)' see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in
Heaven ."'
Those are not my words; they were written by our Past Grand Master
Edgar V. Stewart, Jr. who served as leaderof our Fraternity in 1955. My brethren,
those words are just as true today as they were when Grand Master Stewart spoke
them . In 1955, there were 224,887 members of California Lodges. Members hip
increased in 244,586 in 1965, the high water mark. There were 709 Californi a
Lodges. Today there are 110,000 Masons who are members of 423 Lodges in
California .
This decline in membersh ip is matched by a decline in membersh ip of
many of our concorda nt bodies. Un fortunately the pattern has been fairl y unifonn
throughou t the United States. This d ecline has not been limited to our Fraternity
but has been felt even more strongly in many other fraternal organizations. Indeed,
some have even ceased to exist.
There are many stated causes for this loss of interest in fraternal
organizat ions as well as service clubs. Whatever the cause, our Fraternity has lost
a whole generatio n of young men who matured in the 1960's and l 970's whose

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

source of pleasure and pride to me to participate in degree work and to the
ceremonies of our opening and closing. It is a source of great satisfaction to many ,
and it is always pleasing to discover the intellectual prowess and acuity of many
of our brethren who for one reason or another were not able to acquire as much
fonnal education as others.
What then is the answer? We all wish we knew and there have been amn y
suggestions offered. Almost without exception, there is a lively discussion in
every Lodge after every meeting during which proposals are debated and solutions
reached. The only difference between those who participate in those discussions
and come up with the answers and this Grand Master is that I am charged in our
Constitution with being the leader of this organization. It is my responsibility
under the oath I took when I was installed to do my best for the health of this
Fraternity.
A leader has sometimes been defined as someone who detennines which
way the troops are advancing and then runs around and gets in front. I would be
happy to be that kind of a leader if I could only figure out which way you brethren
are moving. The fact of the maner is, despite my repeated requests for input, and
there has been significant input, I am able to detennine no clear concensus among
you.
For that reason , I have detennined to take the initiative on my own and
propose a solution which I have done in my Recommendation No. I. You will
hear me talk further on this subject tomorrow when I discuss the pros and cons
with you but believe me brethren, Recommendation No. I is the result of a lot of
prayerful thought, consideration of the input offered to me, and the knowledge
gained in talking to everyone and anyone willing to discuss the subject with me.
I believe Recommendation No. l is something that can achieve the desired
objective without throwing out the baby with the bathwater. Clearly there are
objections to the elimination of the proficiency examination. The most frequently
astated is that, ''I learned it, let them do it too" but more about that tomorrow. In
the meantime, please rest assured that I will oppose any effort to change or dilute
our core principles. Brethren, love, relief, truth, morality and integrity are the
foundation stones of our Brotherhood yesterday, today and forever. Those core
values are not a goal but are our very reason for being.
One other major emphasis I have undertaken this year has been to stress
the unity of our Blue Lodges and our concordant and appendant bodies. There is
a synergy which we can achieve by the realization that we are all brothers and
sisters, working together under the same principles and striving for the same
objectives. One of the most successful events of the year was the Unity Day
Ceremony held at the magnificent Al Malaikah Shrine Temple in Los Angeles. My

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

1998/99 SPECIAL GRAND LODGE PER CAPITA

My brethren, I am therefore asking you, I am therefore pleading with you
to agree to a $1.00, one year only additional per capita tax to be used solely for the
purpose of a professional public re lations campaign. If you do so, we wi ll have a
.
I .
base of $100,000.00 with which to begin th is program. The organizations I
refe rred to above have ind icated that they wi ll each contribute an additional
$100,000.00. In today's costs, this is little enough to begin the campaign, but I wil I
promise you that I wi ll not come to you any fu rth er th is year or at the end of my
year as Grand Master, 1998/99, if I am fortuna te enough to be elected by you, to
ask you for any addition a l funds. If they are needed, we w ill fi nd them. I
guarantee you we will find them.

FOR PROFESSIONAL P UBLIC RELATION USE
As I travel up and down the State o f California a nd for that matter
elsewhere, I find that the crying need of all Masons is for instruction and assistance
in how to enlarge and restore our membership. Many ways have been suggested,
some innovative, some just plain hard work. When I have suggested the idea of
a professional public relations firm that will be hired to "get our light out from
under the bushel" and spread the word of Freemasonry to the community at large,
my comments are continuously interrupted by applause, sometimes standing,
among the brethren . Whether at the Junior Wardens' Retreats, at the
Administrative Seminars, among the Inspectors or just in speaking at Lodges and
groups of our appendant and concordant bodies, the acclamation is resounding.
We need a professional public relations program. We want a public relations
program .
Our present Grand Lodge Public Relations Committee works very hard
and very diligently with limited resources, limited time and limited ex perience to
perform the job for us. But they are limited . Professiona l ass istance is desired.
Professional assistance is required if we are going to get the job done.
No ma n is going to join an organization that he doesn't know exists. No
man is goi ng to join a n organization that he knows little about, and what little he
may know may be the re sult of negative comments and criticism by those from
without the fraternity.
I have discussed this with many of you, and have discussed the financial
needs in this regard in order to implement the program. 1 am pleased and proud to
say that at least two of our appendant and concordant bodies have indicated a
willingness to join us in this program with a substantia l contr ibution of funds. It
is necessary that we meet their commitment.
Unfortunately the norma l funds of the Grand Lodge are not sufficient to
afford this fund . Some are too limited in scope to give us the broadness that we
need in a good publicity campaig n, and others just don ' t have the money.
I send thi s letter to you separate and apart from my other comments with
respect to per capita since I feel this is an important letter for you to read and
discuss with your members. It's go ing to cost money. Nobody likes to spend
money. Nobody likes to be taxed, including me. But I think each of us is willing
to do a little bit more if the need is signified to promote o ur frate rnity. We can do
no less if we are go ing to have our fraternity after the next severa l years.

But we need your commitment now . We need your support when I
propose th is assessment at our next Grand Lodge Communication. I know we can
count on you. I know the fraternity can coun t on you because our survival
demands it.
God bless you for your support and God bless you for the sacrifice that
you are going to make in this regard as part of our concept of "shared sacrifice".

Letter ofAugust 19. 1997
to All Lodge Secretaries

REPORT OF THE GRAND TREASURE R

To the Most Worshipful Grand l odge. F.& A.M. of California:

The Grand Treasurer is charged with the responsibility of reporting on the
financial condition of Grand Lodge and its related investments, businesses and
charities at the Annual Communication. This includes the financial statements,
operations and planning for Grand Lodge, as well as for those of the Masonic
Homes of California. the Masonic Homes Pooled Income Fund, the California
Masonic Retirement Plan, the California Masonic Foundation. the California
Masonic Memorial Temple. and the Nob Hill Masonic Management , Inc . (please
refer to the opinion letters attached in the annual Proceedings by your auditors).
The reports and comments of the Grand Treasurer are based on the official
examinations and statements of our Certified Public Accountants whose reports are
an integral part of the Grand Treasurer's Report. Their audits cover the years most
recently ended and contain both a complete statement of assets under management
as well as a record of the income and expenses for the period.
As delegates to the Annual Communication. you are. in effect, the
shareholders of Grand Lodge and its entities. You are encouraged. and it is
recommended therefore, that you read and review this report. Your observations
are appreciated .•
Both the Grand Lodge and each of its related entities are in sound
financial condition. The extent and size of our investments, businesses, and most
importantly our charitable activities were financially possible in large measure due
to the generosity of prior generations. To ensure the future of these fine programs,
we must continue our Masonic tradition of financial support.
Respectfully submitted.
Thomas C. Holm, Grand Treasurer

1. DESCRIPTION OF mE PLAN:
General
The California Masonic Retirement Plan (the Plan) is a defined benefit plan that provides
retirement ben.etits for substantially all employees of Muonic Homes of California, Maoor1ic Grand
Lodge and Component Organizationa (collectively, the Grand Lodge) who have readied the age
of 21 and completed one year of serviee. It is 111bject to the provisions of the Employee Retirement
Income Security Act of 1974 (ERJSA). Participants should refer to the Plan's docwnents for a more
complete description of the Plan.
Employees with five or more years of service are entitled to annual pension benefits beginning at
normal mimnmt age (65). For MrYice prior to January 1, 1993, the annual Nlimnent benefit at
normal retirelllent is equal to 2 pa-cent of the average annual compensation earned during the five
calendar yan prior to January l , 1993, tiiNs years ol MrYice through 1992. For ..me. after
December 31, 1992. the annual retinment benefit at normal retirement is equal to 2 percent ol the
compensation earned in each full and partial year of serW:-e.
The Plan permits early retirement at ages 55 to 64 for participanta with a minimwn of 10 yan of
serviee. Married employees may elect to receive their pension benefits in the form ol a joint and
survivor annuity. U employees tmninate before rendering five yan of oervice, they forfeit the
right to recwiw the portion of their aa:wnulated plan benefita attributable to the Grand Lodge's
contnlrutiona.
U an active employee dies at age 55 or older, a death benefit equal to the value of the employee's
ICCUlllWated ttqilired contributions is paid to the employee'• beneficiary. A death benefit will also
be payable to an employee who dies after acxwnlliating five years of serviee. Active employees
who become disabled and totally incapacitated may recwive an annual disability benefit that is
equal to the normal retirement benefits they haw ICCUlllWated u of the time they becmne disabled,
reduced for -ly withdrawal Disability benefits are paid until normal retirement age, at which
time disabled participants begin receiving normal retirement benefits.

The assets ol the Plan are maintained in a trust established pursuant to a trust agreement between
the Grand Lodge and Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.
Funding Policy
Prior to January 1, 1982, contributions to the Plan had been made by participating employers and
employees baled upon a percentage of covered payroll. Effective January l, 1982. the requirement
for employee contributions was terminated. The Grand Lodge contributes actuarially determined
amounts sufficient to amortize the unfunded present value of aa:umlliated plan benefits over the

-4-

working lifetime of the active participonb. The Plan c:oinplies with the miniznum funding
requiranents of ERISA.
Plan TenNn.ation

Although the Grand Lodge hu no intention to terminate the Plan. it hu the ability to do oo.
Showd the Plan terminate at oome future time, its net uoets generally will not be available on • pro
rata basis to provide participonts' benefits. Whether a particular participanrs accumlliated plan
benefits will be paid depends on both the priority of thoee benefits and the level of benefits
guaranteed by the Pension Bendit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) at that tiiN. Some benefits may
be fully or partially provided for by the then-existing uoets and the PBGC ggaranty, while other
benefits may not be provided for at all.
Information about the plan agreement. the vesting ond benefit provisiona, ond the PBGC • benefit
guaranty is available from the Grand Lodge.

167

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRET ARY

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

My Brethren,
This is the sixth report that I have made to Grand Lodge. The past year
has been an active one for the Grand Lodge Office, and the principle activities may
be summarized as follows:
New Membership Department Database
With the change from a DOS-based operating system to Windows95, it
became necessary to replace the former Membership Department Database with
a new one. Staff members have worked with the consulting firm which is
designing the software to meet our unique needs. The new system is expected to
be in place shortly after January l, 1998.
Secretaries' Meetings
We continued to hold six workshops each spring to help our lodge
secretaries become more effective in their role as the chief administrative officer
of the lodge. Workshops were held in San Diego, Riverside, Los Angeles, Fresno,
Sacramento, and San Jose. In addition, two workshops for new secretaries were
held, one in the north and one in the south. In 1996 the customary workshop was
held on the Saturday before Grand Lodge. However, as Saturday, October I l,
1997 fell on Yorn Kippur, the workshop was not held this year at Grand Lodge.
Secretaries' Associations
Secretaries' associations continue to be an important link with our lodges.
There are currently nine of them which are active, and eight of these meet
quarterly. Some staff member from Grand Lodge was present at each of these
meetings. Joel Springer, my Executive Assistant, shared the responsibility with
me, to attend these meetings. Although run by their own elected officers, these
associations provide an excellent opportunity for interaction with our secretaries,
and an opportunity to improve communication between the Grand Lodge Office
and our lodges.

PROCEEDrNGS OF THE

. GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Boards and Committees
As Grand Secretary I also serve as corporate secretary to the Masonic
Homes Board, the Board of the California Masonic Memorial Temple, the Nob
Hill Masonic Management Board of Directors, and the Board of Trustees of the
California Masonic Foundation. In addition, I serve as secretary to the Executive
Committee, and to several other committees of Grand Lodge. Attendance at these
meetings requires extensive travel throughout the state, but it also affords me an
opportunity to meet with key leaders of the Craft to devote so much of their time
to our boards and committees. My appreciation is expressed to the trustees of our
boards, and to our committee members, for the harmonious working relationship
with the Grand Lodge Office staff who assist them with their duties.

EXHIBITS AND REPORTS

168

Membership Statistics
as of June 30, 1997

Membership Statistics
The number of lodges in our jurisdiction continues to decline, with many
consolidations again this year. There were 424 lodges on the roll of the Grand
Lodge as of June 30, 1997. A year ago on that same date there were 437 lodges,
a loss of 13 lodges. In 1996 we had 110,227 Master Masons listed as members of
our constituent lodges. In 1997 we have l 05,553. Out net membership was 4,674
less than the previous year. We raised 817 new Master Masons in 1997, but lost
3 ,509 members due to deaths, and 1,547 were suspended for non-payment of dues.
It should be clear that with a gain of 817 new Master Masons, and a loss of 1,547
due to suspensions for non-payment of dues, we are in trouble. There is nothing
that we can do about the losses due to death, but we should take a serious look at
the losses due to suspension for non-payment of dues.

Grand Secretary

Summary
Freemasonry in California is going to be challenged in the years ahead as
never before. If we are to stem the tide of the loss of lodges, and the loss of
members, we must be willing to work together to make Freemasonry in California
the strong, vibrant, significant organization that we want it to be. The Grand
Lodge Office is pledged to doing its part to make that happen, and with the
leadership of our other Grand Lodge Officers, I firmly believe that we will do so.

Respectfully submitted,
John L. Cooper III, PM

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER

Most Worshipful Brethren:
At the outset I take this opportunity to thank you for pennitting me to
serve as Grand Lecturer.
.
The Inspector's Annual Reports have been received and thoroughly
reviewed. The temptation is great to distort the "picture", however, the facts are
as follows.
Since our last Communication we lost another 5,500 members and 15
Lodges. Our Lodges are hurting for officers and are relying on Past Masters to
assist in keeping them going. Thirty-four percent of the three principal officers
(the Master, Senior and Junior Wardens) are Past Masters. We appreciate and
thank them for their tenacious spirit, realizing of course, that this is a short lived
solution.
Of course, there are exceptions. Some Lodges are doing well, but they are
rare.
Nineteen seminars were conducted throughout the jurisdiction during the
year, and we than you for your interest with your attendance.
In closing, I say to our Grand Master and his lovely Clara, please accept
my sincerest and P.rofoundest thank you for the rapport I have enjoyed this year
with you.
To the other Grand Lodge Officers for your attendance at our ceremonies
and receptions, and for being so receptive to our instructions ... we thank you.
To our Grand Secretary and his entire staff, many thanks for your
assistance whenever we needed it.
To the Inspectoral Corps, all I 03 of you, thank you, thank you, thank you
for all the time and service you give to our Fraternity.
To all our coaches, for your time, patience and perseverance, a grateful
Fraternity says thank you.
To my colleagues on the Ritual Committee for all the service, assistance
and courtesies, you have my sincerest thank you.
And to you my brethren, for making it all possible ... thank you.
Respectfully submitted,
Ulysses G. Patropulos, Grand lecturer

GRAND CHAPLAI N'S MESSAGE

Devotional Service
Invocation
Our heavenly Father, we have gathered here in this great cathedral erected
in your name. We have joined together, we of many faiths, to give thanks and
praise to you for your presence in our daily lives. This service is a reminder of the
Masonic tenet of Brotherly Love. We pray that the whole world may learn from
our example that Brotherly Love can unite peoples of every country, sect and
opinion and cause true friendship to exist among those who might otherwise have
remained at a perpetual distance. All this we ask in your name. AMEN.

Scripture Readings
Our scripture readings come from the Holy Writings sacred to those of the
Islamic, Jewish and Christian faiths.
Our first reading is the 103n1 Surah, The Declining Day, from the Koran,
sacred to those oflslam:
In the Name ofAllah, the Compassionate, the Merciful
I SWEA'R. by the setting sun that eternal damnation shall be the fate of
everyone, except for those who have faith and do good works and exhort
each other to justice and fortitude.
The prophet Micah speaks similarly to those of the Jewish faith:
He has showed you, 0 man, what is good;
and what does the Lord require of you
but to do justice, and to love kindness,
and to walk humbly with your God?
For Christians, Matthew recites a story teaching the same truths:
[A] lawyer ... asked Hirn a question, to test Hirn. "Teacher, which is the
great commandm ent in the law?" And He said to him, "You shall love
the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with al I
your mind. This is the great and first commandment. And a second is

200

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

like it, You shall love your neighbor as yourself.
commandments depend all the law and the prophets."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

On these two

Whether we are Islamic, Jewish or Christian, the message for each of us
is the same: faith and love light our pathway back to God.
Today's readings from the sacred writings were taken from only three of
world's religions, but it could just as easily been taken from three others, as faith
and love are central themes in all religions.
It is shared values that have been the cornerstone of Freemasonry.
Regardless of our religious beliefs, we can all agree on the practice of the cardinal
virtues of temperance, fortitude, prudence, and justice. As well as the principle
tenets of our craft, Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth.
The eternal question facing every religious person, is what does it take to
be true and faithful to your religion? Our craft faces a similar question, what does
it take to be a Mason?
I think that Dr. Joseph Fort Newton, a noted Masonic author and
clergyman and the Grand Chaplain oflowa from 1911 to 1913, spoke eloquently
on what a Mason is, when he said, "A Mason stands for the right of a soul to know
the truth and to look up unhindered from the lap of earth into the face of God. Not
freedom from faith, but freedom of faith. The emphasis of Masonry is upon the
building of character and the practice of righteousness, upon that moral culture
without which man is rudimentary,and that spiritual vision without which intellect
is the slave of greed or passion. What makes a man great and free here or
anywhere is loyalty to the laws of right, of truth, of purity, of love, and the lofty
will of God." While Brother Newton speaks of the definition of what a Mason is,
how does a Mason determine that he is living by this lofty standard?
As the Grand Lodge has traveled around the state this year, our Grand
Orator has spoken about many people, some that were Masons, and some that were
not. What each of these people has had in common was their service to others.
They didn'tjust recite a list of virtues or tenets, they acted them out. Their actions
in doing something for others demonstrates the tenet that we call Brotherly Love.
As many of you know, I have been a police officer for the City of Los
Angeles for 23 years. In my professional life, I have come in contact with
countless people who have claimed they had high moral values and yet when
tempted by greed or avarice have sho~n themselves to be of the lowest morals. It
is easy to say you have high moral values, it is quite another to demonstrate them
by your actions. The real test of ones moral values is when you are tempted, when
no one else could ever know that you have stolen something and you don't do it,
then you have demonstrated your true moral values.

201

To be a good Mason, it is not how many degrees you have taken, nor how
many offices you have held, nor how many honors you have received, nor the
obligations you have memorized that makes you a Mason. It is how you act in
your daily life, whether it is in your professional, personal or Masonic activities,
that show you are a Mason. How you treat others tells them what your values
really are. It is based on this principle that some Grand Lodges, have from time to
time, made a man a Mason on sight. These men thus made have shown by their
actions, by their life long commitment to the ideals we hold dear, that nothing
remains to make them a Mason, but the declaration by the brethren that they were
a brother and a Mason. Can the same be said of every Mason? Are we living our
lives in keeping with our Masonic ideals? Could we be made a Mason on sight,
based upon our actions alone? This is the daily challenge each of us faces and
meeting this challenge is how we demonstrate our love and faith as true Masons.
May each of us live our lives upon a foundation of faith in God, using the
square of justice, the plumb line of rectitude and the extended points of the
compass that restrain the passions, so that everything we do in our daily lives will
be true to our ideals and bring honor to our craft and glory to your holy name.
Let us pray.
Benediction
Our heavenly Father, we give thanks to you for this great country of ours and for
our noble fraternity. We have dedicated ourselves to your service and pray that
each of us in our daily lives may practice the virtues of temperance, fortitude,
prudence and justice. We pray that our actions, inspired by your spirit, may serve
to maintain in their fullest splendor, those truly Masonic ornaments, Brotherly
Love, Relief and Truth. All this we ask in your name. AMEN.

GRAND ORATIO N

Ronald L. Koretz, Grand Orator
Quality = Making A Difference
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Past Grand Masters, my fellow Grand
Lodge Officers, distinguished visitors from other Grand Jurisdictions, members of
Grand Lodge, and, most importantly, my brothers:
The charge of the Grand Orator at this time is to deliver an address upon
matters appertaining to the craft. For the past year, our Grand Master has traveled
around the state of California emphasizing his theme: "Quality is the Key - You
Can Make a Difference!" Hence, for 1996-97, the issue of making a difference has
been a matter appertaining to the Craft. My remarks to you today will reflect on
that topic.
First of all, on behalf of all of this year's appointed and elected line, I
would like to thank Most Worshipful Alan B. Gresham for his efforts in leading
Grand Lodge. His work has most certainly made a difference in improving the
direction and image of Masonry in California. On a personal note, I must thank
him for the opportunity he provided me to participate in this process. As one who
was permitted to ~are some of the public spotlight, I must thank the other Grand
Lodge Officers, as well as all of our ladies, for their ideas and words of
encouragement, and acknowledge their hard work and personal sacrifices behind
the scenes. But, perhaps most importantly, I must thank the people whose stories
inspired me during the past year. These were all individuals who, in their unique
ways, made differences in their own communities. I was able to use many of these
stories in local addresses, and I would like to share four of them with you in a
symbolic trip around a lodge room.
We will start in the East. Its symbol is the Square, the emblem of virtue.
Last October, the Grand Lodge officers were in San Jose for two separate
events. In the time between them, the Grand Chaplain and I walked around the
Scottish Rite Building. We met an elderly gentleman who was rolling up old
newspapers in one of the storage rooms. The man was Bill Nelson, an 82-year-old
Past Master of Palo Alto-Roller Lodge #346. For the past 11 years, Bill has been
raising money for the Scottish Rite by using donated newspapers Rite to make 25
pound rolls of double-sheeted paper. In order to do so, he had to open each
newspaper, separate out and remove the single sheets, and then place the remaining
double sheets one on top of another, each one slightly offset from the one below.

206

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

When 25 pounds of paper were so stacked, he rolled the pile up. Thus prepared,
the paper could be sold to wholesale florists for $180/ton, netting an extra $170/ton
over what the paper alone was worth. It took Bill an hour to make one roll, for
which the Scottish Rite received an additional $2. Bill estimated that his project
brought in about $3000 each year. In other words, he dontated about 30 hours per
week to this project.
The issue was not the money. There are certainly many people who could
simply write a check for $3000 and not think anything about it. The issue is that
Bill provided his time and his energy; his work was an act of love. It would be
nice to think that the flowers that were subsequently wrapped in that paper became
a little brighter or stayed fresher for a little while longer.
Bill Nelson showed me that you're never too old to contribute to your
community. He taught me to measure the virtue of charity not by the size of the
monetary donation, but by the sire of the donor's heart.
The South is the station of the Plumb, a symbol of moral rectitude, of
doing the right thing, if you will.
Jerry and Sally Freeman live in Los Angeles. For the past 36 years, they
have cared for over 200 very special foster children. Each one of these children
was afflicted with some major physical handicap, defects which usually cause
people to become uncomfortable and tum away.
Some time ago, they were asked to take a 5 month old boy, Jacob, into
their home. Jacob had a progressivedegeneratingneurologicdisorder, and he was
not expected to live for more than a year. After a great deal of soul-searching, the
Freemans accepted Jacob and made the decision that, for however long he was
alive, Jacob's quality of life would be as good as this couple could make it. As
Jacob developed, it became apparent that he would need some surgerical
procedures if he was ever going to be able to walk on his own. Initially, the
doctors balked at doing anything. They believed that the long term gains, which,
given his life expectancy, were mostly hypothetical anyway, would not outweigh
the short term pain the surgeries would cause. Sally Freeman saw the situation
differently; to her, Jacob needed the surgery to improve his ambulatory capacity,
and thus his independence and quality of life. She ultimately prevailed, and the
surgeries were done.
I met the Freemans this past spring, when my own lodge presented them
with an award for their years of compassionate work. Sally told us that, after the
orthopedic procedures, he did learn to ambulate independently. She told us that,
while his disease had limited his verbal development, he had learned to
communicate using a computer. She told us that the neurologic process had

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

207

progressed to the point where he now needed a walker or wheel chair to get
around.
Most importantly, she told us that Jacob had recently celebrated his fourth
birthday.
The Freemans gave love and compassion to another human soul. The
consequence was an outcome that was betterthan would have occurred otherwise.
They did the right thing.
We find the Level in the West. It is a symbol of equality.
Arnold Astrada was a Green Beret in 1981 when he made a practice
parachute jump from an airplane at 1200 feet. The exercise became anything but
routine when the chute failed to open. He survived the ordeal, but he was left
permanently paralyzed from the waist down and confined to a wheel chair. After
working his way through a major depression, he focussed his attention on wheel
chair athletics, the shot-put in particular. He went to the Wheel Chair PanAmerican Games in 1986 and won the Gold Medal. He took the Silver Medal in
the Wheel Chair Olympic Games in Seoul in 1988 and again in Barcelona in 1992.
He returned from Spain determined to win the Gold when the Games came to
America in 1996.
In 1993, he developed a lung condition and his doctors told him that he
woud never compete again. Somewhat later, he met with two other wheel chair
athletes, both of whom he had coached in the past. The three of them made a pact
to compete in Atlanta in 1996 together. They went to the US trials in San Diego
in 1996, where tragedy struck. Both of Arnold's friends died there, one day apart.
Grief stricken, Arnold made the team and vowed to represent all three of them in
Georgia. Shortly after arriving in Atlanta, his lungs again began to act up, and he
also found out that he had a broken bone in his shoulder. Nonetheless, Arnold
believed that he had to compete. So, burdened by these additional emotional and
physical problems, he went out and put the shot.
He won the Gold Medal.
There is a metaphor regarding Effort which is appropriate for this story
and for the Level in the West. It is: "We all have the same sky, but we all don't
have the same horizon."
The North has no station or symbol. In Masonry, it is a place of darkness.
Alex Swan was the Grand Chaplain in 1992-93. I met him at that time,
and we became good friends. He even became an officer in my lodge. A man in
his 80's, he was a practitionerofChristian Science. This religious pursuit accepts
the existence of Divine healing, and its adherents do not seek what much of the rest

208

209

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of the world would view as traditional medical care. It was hard to argue with his
choice of health care, because, even at his age, he was so robust and cheerful.

they believed in. It was only as an incidental side effect that they became
inspirations.
So it is with each ofus. In our day-to-day lives, we do not do what we do
simply to make a difference to others. Nonetheless, we wind up making
differences all of the time. For example, small acts of kindness or anger are
magnified in the recipient. Have you ever been driving on the road and had
someone let you in ahead of him or her? When that happens, it creates a warm
sensation in you that far outlives the few seconds you saved at the time. On the
other hand, when someone suddenly cuts you off, it sets up a negative feeling that
lasts far longer than the delay incurred when you had to step on the brakes. I
would suggest that, in both instances, other people made differences to you.

It is important to understand this background because of the events that
accompanied the last few months of his life. During that time, his health did
decline, and it was during this period that he had his most profound impact upon
me.
It is easy, in the abstract, to talk a good fight. It is another matter entirely
when one actually has to fight it. Alex had a stroke. While he initially appeared
to make a satisfactory recovery, he subsequently developed major problems with
his respiration; he spent the last many weeks of his life being short of breath all of
the time.
I would ask all of you, for a moment, to put yourself in such a condition.
Just hold your breath long enough to experience the mild anxiety that occurs as
your body becomes oxygen deprived. Now imagine that anxiety not going away.
That is akin to how Alex felt. As a traditional physician observing him, I
concluded that Alex had heart failure, and I believed that there were medical
interventions available which would allow him to breathe with much less effort.
I am sure he knew the same. Many people would find it easy to trade an abstract
religious conviction for such an opportunity to breathe more comfortably. Alex
never succumbed to that temptation; he remained true to his belief.
In what proved to be one of the last times I talked to him, I asked him
what he would want done if he suddenly collapsed in the lodge. This was not an
idle question; if such an event were to happen, I had no doubt that I would be asked
to make the medical decision. His response, given only a few words at a time, was
that he wanted people to pray for him. We were to call his wife, not the
paramedics.
During those months, Alex Swan became, for me, a testament to courage
and belief in one's convictions. While his bodily functions did cease last
November, his spirit will certainly live on, at least in me. I may practice a different
type of health care, but I hope that I can emulate his dignity and faith at the end of
my days.
The North was never dark to Alex Swan. He died with the light of faith.
These stories, as well as many others that I do not have the time to tell, are
all inspiring ones of people who made differences. But why tell them? Yes, they
are inspirational and do exemplify the Grand Master's theme. But I am relating
them to you for another reason.
These people did not behave the way they did with the intent of
impressing others. They did what they did because it was who they were and what

In fact, we can't help but make a difference with each of our actions. If
you stop and think about it for a moment, you will realize that society is nothing
more than a collection of individual people. As such, its behaviors represent the
sum total of each person's behaviors. To provide you with a concrete example, let
me paraphrase the slogan that came out of the anti-litteringcampaign: "Every litter
bit makes a difference."
In this regard, let us consider the society in which we are now living. It
is far different from the one our parents grew up in or that some of us older people
remember from our own youths. Materialism has become our primary focus. We
measure people by what they have, not by how they got it. Self promotion is
taking the place of brotherly love. Greed is replacing relief. Marketing is
overwhelming truth.
I have purposely cited our three principle tenets, because Masonry is one
of the few remaining repositories of what is commonly referred to as "traditional
values". We all have values, although no two of us have exactly the same ones.
Values are the things which you intrinsically desire, the things you go to bat for,
the things that you would describe as being really important in your life.
Through the millenia, human beings became "social animals", that is, they
developed skills and behaviors that allow them to live together for their mutual
benefit. They rely on each other. Such a group of interdependent people must
have certain rules to live by. If they routinely killed each other, or lied to each
other, the social structure would collapse. Hence, traditional values, such as
brotherly love, relief, and truth, are things which society as a whole has found to
be important to promote. They are the things that a society would describe as
being really important for its life.
If you will, these traditional values are biologically important to the
survival of a society ,just as the drive to eat is biologically important to the survival

210

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of the individual. Society, as the ultimate beneficiary of traditional values, will ask
its members to make sacrifices in the interest of this greater good.

Traditional values and materialism are the antitheses of each other, and
they must invariably come into conflict. In such a contest, nobody can sit on the
sidelines. The common peer justification for materialistic behavior is the argument
that "everyone does it". If you remain silent and do not challenge that statement,
it becomes true, at least as far as you are concerned. Even if you do not practice
materialism yourself, being passive gives others the permission to continue.
Hence, if you do not become part of the solution, you will be part of the problem.
To paraphrase Edmund Burke, the only thing necessary for the triumph of
materialism is for supporters of traditional values to do nothing.

But why would an individual make a sacrifice? Because it feels good to
do the right thing. I would suggest that we each have in us a biologic need to do
things to benefit society. Being true to, and fulfilling, these needs produces selfesteem and a sense of worth.
In fact, one could speculate that these social drives are genetically
implanted in us. Young children seem instinctively to know right from wrong.
They trust without question, at least until someone teaches them not to. I would
remind you of the lyrics from a song from the musical South Pacific:
"You've got to be taught to hate and fear,
You've got to be taught from year to year,
It's got to be drummed in your dear little ear,
You've got to be carefully taught."
One could even view these innate drives to act morally and to help others
from a theologic perspective and conclude that their presence represents tangible
proof of the existence of a Supreme Being.
We would all agree that these traditional values are good for the individual
and for society. On the other hand, the pursuit of materialistic values is
detrimental. Materialism is, by its very nature, short-sighted. If a man lies to
obtain some advantage today, who will believe him the next time he speaks? If he
sells all of his heritageand mortgages his future for some transient self-indulgence,
how will he buy the next one? Such short term gains invariably lead to long term
losses.
Moreover, while the practice of traditional values makes us feel good,
there is no innate need to drive an expensive car or wear an expensive watch.
Satisfying materialistic values is biologically unfulfilling. Marketing campaigns
would have us believe that we are what we wear, drive, eat, or tell time with. In
the short term, these campaigns are effective. We begin to believe that the world
really is what it is depicted to be in those commercials. As more and more people
buy into this myth, peer pressure begins to exert itself and the myth becomes a selffulfillingprophecy. However, self-worth is not for sale. If a person does not feel
good about him- or herself, trying to compensate by buying some thing is doomed
to failure. After all, if such a worthless person can obtain it, it really could not be
very valuable. Groucho Marx said it best when he commented that he would
resign from any club that would accept him as a member. Self-esteem is free, but
we have to find it in ourselves, not in our environment.

211

There is a song from the stage play Annje. which provides some insight
into this conflict. At the beginning of the musical, as well as at the end, Annie
sings a song called "Tomorrow". I would like you to think about one of the lines
of that song. In particular, I would ask you to fill in a missing word: "Tomorrow,
tomorrow, I love you tomorrow,you're [fill in the word] a day away". What is that
word?
Those of you who know the play probably thought of one of two different
words. Those words were either "always" or "only". But which is the right
answer? Actually, they both are. In the beginning of the story, Annie is a poor
orphan girl who, while having great dreams, lives in a reality in which they are not
likely ever to come true. These dreams of her tomorrow are always a day away.
At the end, she has found a new family and she is on the verge of achieving those
dreams. Now, tomorrow is only a day away.
The lesson for us relates to the question: When will tomorrow actually
come? To the materialistic mind, it is always a day away. Taking shortcuts and
living only for the moment and beyond one's means pretends that the futur~ will
never come. Inherent in this behavior is the expectation that, at the time of
reckoning, someone else will pay the piper.
For traditionalists, Masons in particular, tomorrow is only that one day
away. In fact, these people will sacrifice in the present to build for that future. Our
ancient brethren created edifices that have stood the test of time; those structures
are still there centuries later. In taking the extra time and effort to get them built
right, some of these men paid a price. Doubtlessly, a few of them fell off a roof
while being engrossed in performing the job correctly.
A colleague of mine had a 94 year old woman as a patient. Every week
he would visit her in a nursing home, and every week she recited the same lengthy
list of complaints. One time, he asked her if there was anything good about being
94. After a brief pause, she said "Yes. There is no peer pressure." Materialism,
through such devices as marketing, creates an artificial peer pressure that keeps
that value system going.

212

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

But peer pressure, like society itself, is simply the net sum of each
person's input. Since each of those people will have an ingrained sense of right
and wrong, each one can be touched and his or her behavior can be changed.
When enough individuals have changed, society changes. Why not use peer
pressure to emphasize traditional values?
This is the real promise of Masonry. Masonry fundamentally deals with
men on a one-on-one basis. We try to provide an environment in which a person
can become better, through his own efforts and with the encouragement, or, in
other words, the peer-pressure, of the rest of us. Our charge is to practice out of
the lodge those great moral duties which are inculcated in it. It is not unreasonable
to expect, even to demand, that non-Masons do the same. These moral duties,
these teachings of our fraternity, these traditional values, are not our property.
Everyone in society shares them. You do not have to be a Mason to be a Mason.
The battle between traditional values and materialism is being waged as
we speak. We cannot remain neutral in it. We can choose to take as much as we
can and hope someone else will pay for it, or we can choose to build for the future.
In making your particular choice, I would remind you that, in two days, tomorrow
will be yesterday. Realize that the sum of each of our choices today will determine
which of the possible tomorrows we all will then look back at. Each of us will
make a difference. You must decide what the difference is that you want to make.
Thank you.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The current code does not place any restriction on the speed with which
a candidate can progress through the degrees. He is limited solely by his ability to
memorize the proficiencies and to recite them before the Lodge. Eliminating these
memorized proficiencies would raise the possibility of conferring all the degrees
in one day, a practice which I do not favor. I am therefore recommending that we
establish a minimum waiting period between each degree, to enable the candidate
to reflect upon what he has experienced, and to provide an opportunity for the
Lodge to instruct the candidate in the meaning behind the ceremonies. I believe
that this "waiting period" should be no less than twenty days. If a man must wait
at least twenty days between each degree, he will have ample opportunity to reflect
upon the meaning of the degree he has received. Also, the Lodge will have the
opportunity to provide for a reasonable amount of candidate education before he
progresses. I am not recommending that such education be mandatory, for I
believe that such should be left to the discretion of each Lodge. However, the
Grand Secretary's Office has available instructional materials which can be used
for candidate education, including booklets containing information for each of the
·
three degrees.

The Grand Master, acting upon the reports and recommendations of his
Inspector, and following his preliminary investigation and an examiniation of the
financial records of Pasadena Lodge No. 272, suspended the Master of that Lodge.
Section I 050c of the California Masonic Code authorizes the Grand
Master to suspend the Master of any chartered Lodge until the next Annual
Communication. This situation involves serious financial irregularities and
therefore the Grand Master's Decision is in accord with our policy and general
purposes.
Decision ADOPTED.
Recommendation No. 1
Elimination of Candidate Proficiencies
The winds of change are blowing across the world of Freemasonry as we
prepare ourselves to enter the next millenium. No change is being discussed more
widely than what should be required of candidates for our degrees, and how
quickly they should progress toward becoming a Master Mason. In some other
jurisdictions candidate proficiencies have been modified or reduced, or even in
some cases, eliminated in their entirety. One has but to look at the "one day
classes" where all three degrees are conferred in one day.

The time has come for our Grand Lodge to make a decision on the
important matter of candidate proficiencies and candidate advancement. We have
far too many Entered Apprentices who fail to advance, partly because they cannot
or will not memorize our lengthy proficiencies. My proposal would restore any
fees that either Entered Apprentices or Fellow Crafts have forfeited, and allow
· them to continue should they so desire. Without the need to memorize a large
quantity of ritual, many, if not most, may choose to become Master Masons.

Grand Lodge has grappled with the issue of changing the candidate
proficiencies several times before, and this year we will consider Carry-Over
Resolution No. 96-05 which would limit the proficiencies to the signs, words,
modes of recognition, and memorization of the Obligation of each degree. I am
laying before Grand Lodge as my Recommendation No. I another option.

If we do nothing we will continue to lose far too many of those who have
voluntarily sought to become Masons, and then found that our extensive
memorization requirements were too much for them. If we make this important
change in our requirements we will commit ourselves to a different way of
instructing our candidates in the future. I believe that the time has arrived to make
this commitment - for the new millenium!

It is my recommendation that we eliminate the traditional concept of a
memorized candidate's proficiency after each of the degrees and substitute for it
instruction in the signs, words, and modes of recognition. The candidate would be
instructed privately, and he would not be required to demonstrate them before the
lodge. In addition, after his Third Degree the newly raised Master Mason would
be taught how to pass a suitable examination using these signs, words, and modes
of recognition, should he wish to visit another Lodge. He would also receive

Recomm endation No. 2
Modification ofAdmission Requirements for Children

This Recommendation is consistent with the overall general purposes of
Grand Lodge in that it encourages membership application and retention.

Entering the Masonic Home for Children

However, the elimination of the proficiencies is not consistent with our
current policy. It is inconsistent with both our policy and general purposes not to
educate our candidates about our prohibition of solicitation.

Over the past ten years the number of applications for our Masonic Home
for Children at Covina has steadily declined. This is a natural result not only of the
decline in membership in our Fraternity in general, but also of the changing needs
of children in society in general. When the Masonic Home for Children was
established, those children admitted were orphans of Master Masons. They were
the sons or daughters of Master Masons who had lost one or both parents due to
accident or illness, and who needed a home because they had none.
Today the children in our Masonic Home for Children at Covina are rarely
children of Master Masons. They are almost always grandchildren, great
grandchildren, or distantly related to a Master Mason. The average age of our
membership, of course, is primarily responsible for this fact. In fact, these children
are more likely the result of broken homes, children who have lived in foster
homes for years, or children who are the victims of abuse and/or neglect. Meeting
the needs of these children is much more challenging today than simply providing
a place to live. Their social and psychological needs are great, and our Masonic
Home has responded by providing them the help they need to become productive
members of our society when they leave.
I believe that it is desirable to broaden our admissions policy to accept
children regardless of their Masonic relationship. Five years ago we began
accepting some children who have no Masonic relationship on a limited basis.
This program was funded by a special bequest left to the Masonic Home for
Children, and assisted by donations of generous brethren who believed that the
Home could serve other children along with those who have some relationship to
a Master Mason. That program, although limited in scope, has been successful.
I believe that it is now time to broaden this program, and accept children who need
what our Home for Children can provide, regardless of the Masonic relationship
of the child.

Report of the Committee on Ritual:

Grand Master's Recommendation No. I would eliminate the need to
memorize the proficiencies entirely, and substitutes for it only a requirement that
the candidate be taught the words, signs, and modes of recognition. He does not
need to demonstrate them in open Lodge, something that is very intimidating to
some men.
In addition, Grand Master's Recommendation No. I requires a waiting
period between the degrees of no less than 20 days. The purpose of this is to
ensure that the candidate has time to absorb what he has experienced, and to allow
time forthe Lodge to teach him the meaning of the degreetha t he has just received.
While the Ritual Committee does not necessarily believe that a waiting period
between degrees is esential, it is in agreement with the Grand Master that learning
the meaning of the degree just received by the candidate is both desirable and
important.
Carry-over Resolution No. 96-05 was submitted by the Ritual Committee
in 1996 as a response to the overwhelming difficulty that our Lodges have in
getting candidates to advance. We consistently lose more than 30% of Entered
Apprentices, who never advance to become Fellow Crafts. At the time it seemed
as if this proposal would meet the serious needs of our Lodges. However, a year's
worth of experience has shown that this solution is not enough. Even requiring the
memorization of the obligations appears to be a major obstacle for the
advancement of candidates.
We now believe that Grand Master's
Recommendation No. I is a better solution to the problem. The Ritual Committee
therefore urges that you vote "yes" for Grand Master's Recommendation No. I.
Recommendation CARRIED-OVER.

§8010. PURPOSE
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California shall control,
conduct, and manage homes, hospitals, and other facilities for the care,
maintenance and support of the aged, indigent or infirm Master Masons,
their wives, widows, and children, and schools for the education of such
children, and grant non-resident assistance instead of admission to the
Homes. In addition. the Board of Trustees may consider for admission
to the Masonic Homes any child without a known blood relationship to

such a relationship is considered. provided that preference for admission

child without a known blood relationship to a Master Mason must be
sponsored by a Lodge subject to the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge.
The Trustees shall establish rules, terms and conditions, subject to the
approval by the Grand Master, governing admissions to the Masonic
Homes of deserving recipients of Masonic charity. They shall pay the
necessary burial expenses of residents of the Homes who die while under
the supervision of the Trustees, in an amount to be determined by them.

are retired and living on a fixed and usually reduced income and consequently it
is often a hardship on many to pay dues; and
WHEREAS, as they have paid their dues faithfully for fifty years in good
times and bad, it is therefore appropriate to relieve them for paying dues for their
remaining years, ifthe Lodge desires.

California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§21080. DISCRETIONARY EXPENDITURES.

A Lodge may:

representatives in attending the communications of
Grand Lodge;

Appropriate from its funds any amount for the

a Golden Veteran's Award recipient:

Appropriate money for floral pieces for an ill or

memory to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund or to
the California Masonic Foundation;

Compensate the Organist;

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of the Resolution seek to pennit Lodges to purchase a life
membership for Golden Veterans' Award recipients due to the fact that nearly all
of them are retired and living on fixed and usually reduced incomes. The
proponents contend that some of these men may have difficulty in paying their
Lodge dues.
This resolution would add to Section 21080-C pennission for a Lodge to
purchase a life membership for a Golden Veteran Award recipient.
Since it is already possible for a Lodge to purchase such a membership for
a retiring Worshipful Master, this proposal merely represents an extension of an
already-establishedGrand Lodge policy. However, one of the general purposes of
Masonry is a life-long committment to the support of a Lodge; if any member is

226

227

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

unable to pay his dues, there are already mechanisms in place and available to him
(dues remission). Hence, having a Lodge purchase a life membership for any of
its members is actually not consistent with the purposes of Masonry.

This is consistent with the way the Opening of Grand Lodge is conducted. The
Ritual Committee therefore urges a "yes" vote on Carry-over Resolution No. 9604.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponen ts of this resolution seek to eliminate the current
proficienc ies and require candidates to recite from memory only the Obligation,
together with the Signs and Modes of Recognition of each degree. They are also
including a provision for the automatic restoration of previousl y forfeited fees of
Entered Apprentices and Fellowcrafts who have failed to advance.
When one thinks of all the reasons for becoming a Mason, the lengthy
proficiencies now required would not be one. The signs and obligations, on the
other hand, represent the essence of what a Masonic committm ent is.
Many other jurisdictio ns have adopted the practice of employin g a
proficiency test that is limited to the signs and obligations. They have not suffered
from these actions, and may even have benefited.
However there is a potential problem with eliminating the Third Degree
Proficiency. This is the only occasion in our Ritual in which the candidate receives
instruction relating to the unwritten law prohibiting solicitation. However, this
concern is easily remedied as stated by the Grand Lecturer in the Ritual Committe e
Report on Grand Master's Recommendation.
Also, the proposed revision to Section 26330 automatically restores the
candidate who has failed to present himself for advancement. It should be
appreciated that this would be done without notice or investigation by the Lodge.
This Recomme ndation is consistent with the general purposes of Grand
Lodge relating to improving membership retention. However, it is not consistent
with our policy and general purposes not to educate our candidates about our
prohibition of solicitation.

Resolution 96-07
Permits Committees to Make Recommendations
The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit each committee of Grand Lodge
to report its recommendation regarding proposed Grand Lodge action on business
referred to the committee.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M of California:
WHEREAS, it has been the policy of this Grand Lodge for many years,
1993 through 1995 excepted, to permit all Committees to which matters before the
Grand Lodge have been referred to include in their reports recommendations which
they believe appropriate to preserve or enhance the integrity of the established
policies and general purposes of Freemasonry in California;
WHEREAS, in the years 1993 through 1995, our Grand Lodge was
inconsistent in both policy and practice by permitting some committees to make
recommendations while precluding others from doing so; and
WHEREAS, it is, and should be, the prerogative of the members of this
Grand Lodge to determine the proper forum by which they receive information to
assist them in making reasoned and rational decisions on the matters presented
them.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 6230 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

§6230. REFERENCE OF BUSINESS.
All business. inclyding Grand Master's decisions and
recommendations. shall be referred to and reported on by one or
more committees before it can be finally acted on by the
members of Grand Lodge, except by their unanimous consent.
All such committees shall report before any vote shall be taken

231

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

in Grand Lodge and may. at their discretion. include in their
reports such recommendationsas they deem appropriate to state
clearly the position of the committee on the matters being
considered. The vote shall be taken upon the business as
originally presented.
Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

.

Prior to 1993, it was the custom of your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes, as part of their report on each piece of pending legislation, to make a
recommendation to the Grand Lodge regarding a "Yes" or "No" vote. Section
6040 of the California Masonic Code, however, in describing the duties of that
committee, states the following: "The Committee on Policy and General Purposes
shall consider and report on matters referred to it as to whether any action taken or
proposed is consistent with the general purposes and policies of Grand Lodge."
Thus, this committee's task is simply to inform the membership of Grand Lodge
as to whether or not the legislation follows current policy or purpose. That section
does not mandate the committee to make any recommendation regarding whether
or not the legislation should be adopted; it is up to the entire membership of Grand
Lodge, through the voting process, to decide whether or not to change its policy or
purpose.
This committee has had the ability to express its opinion about pending
legislation, even 4n the absence of a formal recommendation. This opinion is
usually obvious in the tone and wording of the report. For example, after you have
heard this report, you will know the opinion of this committee.
In 1978, then Grand Master McCaw, in Decision No. 5 noted that, if it
was not in the California Masonic Code, it was not the law. Since CMC Sections
6080 and 6110 do mandate certain committees, the Committees on Charters and
Trial Review, to make recommendations, it follows that it is the official policy of
Grand Lodge that other committees do not have such a directive. While the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes has ceased this practice, other
committees, which only report on occasional pieces of legislation, still sometimes
make recommendations.
Ifcommittees are given the legal responsibilityto make recommendations,
it is probable that their final reports will have to become justifications of those
recommendations, not unbiased discussions of the issues. Objectivity in the
analysis will tend to be even further lost.
Furthermore, several years ago the rules of debate regarding legislation
were changed to allow equal time for the pro and con perspectives. This change
is clearly in the interest of fairness in the discussion of an issue. If committees are

233

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

given official sanction to present a recommendation, there will be disproportionate
representation of one side or the other during the debate.

WHEREAS, the position of Assistant Grand Secretary was discontinued
by vote of Grand Lodge in 1994, along with the position of Assistant Grand
Treasurer;

232

Because of these considerations, in 1993 the official instruction to the
Policy and General Purposes Committee was returned to, and made consistent
with, its original CMC-mandated charge. This is the same mandate under which
the Jurisprudence committee has always operated. Obviously, it would be
inappropriate for that committee ever to express a recommendation, although this
proposed resolution even provides that possibility. It is true that committees which
only report on occasional pieces of legislation do sometimes make
recommendations. Technically, this is an error. It is contrary to our current policy
to allow error to be institutionalized into our law. Two wrongs do not make a
right.

WHEREAS, the experience of the Grand Secretary's Office without an
Assistant Grand Secretary has been less than satisfactory; and
WHEREAS, it is desirable in the opinion of the Grand Secretary to restore
the position of Assistant Grand Secretary as an appointed officer of Grand Lodge.

and 5020 of the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

§540. VACANCY OR INCAPACITY.

Should the offices of the Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Senior and
Junior Grand Wardens all become vacant or all the incumbents become
incapacitated, it shall be the duty of the Grand Secretary or Assistant
Grand Secretaiy to convene a Special Communication within 60 days of
the last occurring vacancy or incapacitation at which members of Grand
Lodge shall be elected and installed in the manner provided for at an
Annual Communication. Pending the election and installation, the
immediate living Past Grand Master shall discharge the duties of the
Grand Master.
