Resolutio n No. 97-01
Permits Monitorial Portions of
Master's Lecture to be Read
The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit the monitorial portions of the
Master's Lectures to be read as well as to be delivered from memory during the
conferral of degrees.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

237

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit the monitorial portions
of the Master's Lectures to be read as well as to be delivered from memory during
the conferral of degrees.

If part of the lecture is memorized and part read, two different tempos can
be created. This may be distracting for the candidate.
The proponents have not provided any proof that reading the lecture will
be better comprehended by the candidate. There is reason to believe that it will not
be. Since one of our primary purposes is to teach our lessons to our candidates,
attempting to do so in the proposed manner is clearly not consistent with our
general purposes.

WHEREAS, Masonry attempts to explain the ethics, history and the true
meaning of the Brotherhood of Man to each new Candidate as he receives his
degrees;

This would be a change in California Masonic Ritual and is not consistent
with current Grand Lodge policy.

WHEREAS, we deem it necessary thatthese lessons be presented, in the
most dignified manner possible, so as to impress upon the Candidate the
seriousness of our intentions;

Report ofthe Committee on Ritual:

WHEREAS, we find that personal demands upon prospective officers
contribute, measurably, to their reluctance to commit themselves to the
memorization of the esoteric as well as the monitorial work;
WHEREAS, in past years, when there were great numbers of conferrals,
the officers had the added opportunity to absorb much of the work by its continual
presentation, which opportunity is denied with the much fewer number of
conferrals;
WHEREAS, it is felt that the reading of the monitorial portions of the
Master's lectures will make a better impression and be better understood by the
candidate, without having interruptions due to necessary prompting; and
WHEREAS, we further feel that the lessening of the demands of this
memorization may gain favorable impression by prospective officers.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Ritual of the Grand
Lodge be amended to perm it the monitorial portions of the Masters' Lectures to be
read as well as to be delivered from memory during the conferral of all three
degrees.

The proponents of this Resolution believe that our Ritual will be improved
by reading it to the candidate. The Ritual Committee believes that this is not true.
If the lecture of each degree is not properly learned in the traditional way, and
delivered effectively from memory to the candidate, the candidate runs a great risk
of not learning the importan tteaching softhe degree which he has just experienced.
Reading the lecture is not as effective as delivering the lecture, and the Ritual
Committee therefore urges a "no" vote on Resolution No. 97-0 I.

and disruptive, to change an apron when changing stations during or between
sections of a degree;
WHEREAS, wearing of the same apron for the duration of the degree
would eliminate this inconvenience and confusion;
WHEREAS, the jewel of the station serves to identify the officer of that
station.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

WHEREAS, a strong implication exists which indicates the JudeoChristian persuasion is to be held in reverence above all other religious bodies;

The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit a Mason to wear the
apron appropriate to his rank or station when occupying an officer's station, so
long as he wears the jewel appropriate to the station he is occupying.

WHEREAS, our Craft teaches that we recognize and accept men of all
faiths, as long as tl'ley believe in a Supreme Being and life hereafter;

This change could raise questions as to which is the appropriate apron for
various stations and is not consistent with Grand Lodge policy.

Report ofthe Committee on Ritual:
The authors of Resolution No. 97-04 would permit any Master Mason
sitting in an officer's station to wear an apron other than the apron of that station.
Presently permission to wear something other than the apron of the station is
extended only to Past Masters, and then only once a year on a Past Masters' Night.
It would thus be possible for an Inspector, a Grand Lodge Officer, or even a visitor
from another jurisdiction, to wear an apron which has nothing to do with the station
being occupied. The Ritual Committee is opposed to this proposal. The apron and
jewel of a station belong together. They are the proper Masonic Clothing of an
officer, and wearing other Masonic aprons which have nothing to do with the
office clouds the symbolism of the office itself. While this might be acceptable
once a year for a Past Master's Night when Past Masters are being honored, it is
!121 appropriate on other occasions. The "jewel and apron" of his office are the

WHEREAS, while most members acquiesced in the past and did not
question the use of the words "Holy Bible" in ritual work, individuals openly
voiced concern about having to refer to their Holy Writings as a "Holy Bible" once
our California Grand Lodge adopted the use of alternate Holy Writings;
WHEREAS, no member, thus far, has objected to use of the term "Holy
Writings" in lieu of the term "Holy Bible";
WHEREAS, our Third Degree lecture begins, "[w]e read in the Holy
Writings that it was decreed in the wisdom and counsels of Deity aforetime, that
a house should be built, erected to God and dedicated to His Holy Name"; and
WHEREAS, the words "Holy Writings" may be substituted for the words
"Holy Bible" everywhere they appear in the Ritual without great difficulty, as the
syllables are the same and changes can be readily made in the Monitor and Cipher
by lining through the word "Bible" and writing in the word "Writings" in the space
immediately above.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Ritual be amended to
substitute the words "Holy Writings" for the words "Holy Bib le" everywhere they
appear.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

adding additional ritual work for our Lodges. Vote "no"!

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The proponents of this Resolution seek to exempt a Brother who has
qualified for an office from having to requalify for the same office for a period of
two years.
To maintain consistency in levels ofleadership, the Inspectornow reviews
the qualifications of the Lodge officers. By eliminating this responsibility, this
Resolution is not consistent with Grand Lodge policy.
Report of the Committee on Ritual:

This Resolution would exempt some officers from the requirement that
they obtain a certificate of proficiency from the Inspector before being installed,
but not others. Those exempted are those that had a certificate from the previous
year. This legislation does not require that an officer be proficient - it merely
requires him to have a certificate showing that at one time he was proficient. The
Ritual Committee believes that this legislation is discriminatory, and potentially
damaging to the Ritual of the Lodge. Either an officer is proficient in the Ritual
or he is not. If he is proficient, the Inspector will issue him a certificate. If he is
not proficient he cannot be installed. Merely holding a certificate from the
previous year does not guarantee that he is proficient. The Ritual Committee urges
you to vote "no" on Resolution No. 97-08.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution are seeking to prevent persons who are
transsexuals from becoming Masons. The Resolution was prompted by an incident
in which a transsexual, born as a male and in the process of adopting the
appearance of a female, was initiated into a Masonic-affiliated 'women's
organization after claiming to be the daughter of a Mason.
There are three ways to determine gender. A genetic definition requires
a chromosomal analysis. Gender may be established by the presence of specific
genitalia. Finally, maleness or femaleness may only be a state of mind; a person
is the gender he or she believes him- or herself to be.
Each of these systems has defects. Chromosoma l analysis is not perfect;
genetic disorders exist which do not permit simple gender classification. Some
medical conditions, such as cancer of the prostate, necessitate castration and
estrogen therapy; how would the terms of this Resolution apply to such a person?
The civil law, and therefore society, has adopted the perspective that
gender is defined by the state of mind of the individual. This state of mind causes
a transsexual to undergo the surgical and medical therapy producing the external
physical changes. Such a person must then, of his or her own volition, separately
seek to make the change in the birth certificate.
This Resolution will only apply to the female to male transsexual; it
would have had no bearing on the case in question, a male acquiring a female
appearance. A male to female transsexual would not apply to a Masonic Lodge
after the fact; any male who, after becoming a Mason, underwent a transsexual
change would have signed the proposed statement truthfully.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

259

But how threatening is such an incident to the fraternity? Should we
change our laws to prevent it? It is dangerous to use generic law to solve isolated
problems. In this case, we would be asking thousands of eligible men to sign a
statementtha t is completely irrelevantto them. We will likely alienate a few in the
process. The presence of such a statement displays paranoia and bigotry, not
justice and brotherhood. Virtually no other organization asks potential members
to take such an oath. It will be embarrassing for many Masons to give such a
petition to a friend or colleague.
There may be some concern on the part of the proposers that transsexuals
are fundamentally immoral. However, there is no scientific evidence that supports
this belief. As Masons, we judge each person's morality on the basis of behavior,
not appearance.
The proposal is inconsistentwith current Masonic policy or practice. Rare
incidents are probably better dealt with on an individual basis. More importantly,
if a person believes himself to be a man and is so accepted in society, is of good
character, and wishes to improve himself through Masonry, we have never denied
that opportunity in the past.

Report ofthe Committee on Ritual:
This Resolution would attempt to define who is a "man" for purposes of
applying for the degrees of Masonry. For centuries Masonic Lodges have had no
trouble deciding wh·o are appropriate candidates for the degrees of Masonry. The
Ritual Committee sees no purpose in changing the time-honored right of a Lodge
to make an intelligent decision as to the meaning of "man" for purposes of
applying for the degrees of Masonry. We urge you to vote "no" on this bizarre
piece of legislation.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

Th~ proponents of this Resolution seek to change the wording in the
Second Sect10n of the Lecture of the Third Degree to correct what they perceive
to be an inconsistency in the appellations of King Solomon and the two Hirams.
As is the case for m~ch of the wording of our ritual, it must be carefully
.
cons1d~red from the perspective that our Masonic forefathers actually meant what
they said and that they had some specific intent in mind when they use the terms
they chose. In this instance, a specific difference in the locations of the
appellations should be noted. The references to Grand Master are in the Third
Section, which serves as a recapitulation of the story. The reference to Master
Mason occurs in the Second Section, when the narration is referring to a situation
that existed at a particular moment. At this time, the temple was still being
constructed and there were no other Master Masons. The title "Grand Master" only
became a necessity when it was desirable to separate the first three Master Masons
from those who followed. This subtle point will be lost if the wording of this
Resolution is adopted.
. . Sinc.e preserving the original intent of the lecture is one of our guiding
principles, this Resolution is not consistent with our current policy and purpose.

Report of the Committee on Ritual:
Changes to our Ritual, no matter who well-intended, must not be made for
light and transient reasons. Our Ritual has come down to us from ancient times
and much of the wording reflects the heritage of centuries. The proponents of thi~
change have not correctly understood the symbolism of our Ritual. While it is
clear that Masonic Tradition teaches us that there were three Grand Masters at the
building of King Solomon's Temple, it also teaches us that they were the only three
Master Masons at that date. The Tradition asserts that there were "Masters", or
"Overseers of the Work", but that they were not Master Masons! That term was
reserved for those who possessed the secrets of a Master Mason, and our Tradition
teaches us that there were three, and only three: Solomon, King of Israel; Hiram,

Resolution No. 97-13
Permits Lodges to Transact Certain Business in Untiled Sessions
The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit Lodges to c_onduct ~portion_ of
a Stated Meeting in an untiled session, thereby possibly starting the tiled portion
of Stated Meeting at a time later than that established in the By-laws.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

WHEREAS, a portion of a Lodge's Stated Meeting consists of informal
reports of Youth Orders activities, Sunshine Committees, Event Committees, and
· the like that do not include formal Lodge business;
WHEREAS, giving these informal reports at the pre-Stated Meeting
Dinner may cause the tiled Lodge Meeting to start later than the time stated in a
Lodge's By-laws; and
WHEREAS, it is not desired to have this situation constitute a postponed
Stated Meeting.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 16030 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

§16030. STATED MEETINGS.
A Lodge shall hold a Stated Meeting for the transaction of its regular
business once in each calendar month, except that Lodges whose Bylaws provide for meetings fixed by the phase of the moon shall hold a
Stated Meeting each lunar month.
A Lodge may be opened for a Stated Meeting prior to the time fixed in its
By-Laws. No business shall be transacted prior to such time.
A Stated Meeting may commence prior to the opening of the Lodge. or
after the Qpened Lodge has been called from labor to refreshment. for the
sole pm:pose of presenting reports which do not regujre a vote of the
Lodge. Such reports may include Youth Order reports. reports on Lodge
or other Masonic activities. reports on absent members. reports from the
Masonic Temple Association which do not involve financial or other
confidential matters and reports on departed brethren. Topics of general
interest to the audience may also be reported on and discussed during
such an untiled session. However. in no event may there be reports or
discussions during an untiled portion ofa Stated Meeting which involve
membership applications or member discipline. reguire a vote or disclose
Lodge finances or other confidential matters. Such an untiled ses ion may
occur prior to the time fixed in the Lodge's By-laws and may extend past
the time fixed in its By-laws for the start of the tiled Stated Meeting. A
report of all activities during the untiled portion of the Stated Meeting
shall be included in the minutes of the Stated Meeting.
The Inspector may grant a dispensation to change the date of a Stated
Meeting, as provided for elsewhere in this Code.

264

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

In the event that the Master of a Lodge detenn in es that inclement weather,
including ice, snow, and flood conditions, existing on the day established
in the By-Laws of the Lodge for its Stated Meeting, makes it hazardous
for members of the Lodge to attend the meeting, he may, with the consent
of the Inspector of the District to which the Lodge is assigned, postpone
the Stated Meeting to the same day of the week next following the week
scheduled for the Stated Meeting. Upon such postponing, the Master
shall notify, to the extent possible, all members of the Lodge residing
within 50 miles of the meeting place of the Lodge.
Should a Stated Meeting be postponed, the business transacted at the
postponed Stated Meeting shall be limited to the reading of the minutes
of the last Stated and subsequent Special Meetings, action thereon,
payment of the invoices of the Lodge, and such other business of an
emergent nature as detennined by the Master to require immediate
consideration. No other new business shall be considered.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to pennit Lodges to transact
certain business in untiled sessions. They propose that prior to the opening of the
Lodge, or after Lodge is opened and then called from labor to refreshment, that
certain reports that do not require a vote of the Lodge, may be made. Also, topics
of general interest to the audience may be reported on and discussed during such
an untiled session. The proposal provides that in no event may there be reports or
discussions during an untiled portion of the Stated Meeting which involve
membership applications or member discipline which require a vote, or which
disclose Lodge finances or other confidential matters. A report of all activities
during the untiled portion of the Stated Meeting shall be included in the minutes
of the Stated Meeting.
We find this proposed change is not consistent with current Grand Lodge
policy.

Report of the Committee on Ritual:
Resolution No. 97-13 is unnecessary. Lodges can presently do everything
in an untiled location, such as a dining room, that the proponents are suggesting.
Lodges can report on sickness and distress in an untiled gathering, they can report
on activities of interest to members and guests alike, and they can discuss topics
of general interest to members and friends. All that this legislation does is to
confuse something which is now clear to almost everyone. We should not try to
confuse our Lodges by making needless distinctions between "tiled" business and

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

265

"untiled" business. The Ritual Committee believes that our Lodges are quite
capable of making such intelligent decisions on their own without being told by
Grand Lodge how to run their own affairs. Vote "no" on Resolution No. 97-13!
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.
Resolution No. 97-14
Establishes Rules/or the Hiram Award
The proponents of this Resolution seek to establish qualifications and procedures
for bestowing the Hiram Award.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
WHEREAS, while Masonic Lodges and the Grand Lodge recognize the
Hiram Award and have awarded such with a certificate, medallion and lapel pin
available through Grand Lodge, there is no actual criteria established for the award;
WHEREAS, there has been no clear guidance on the award, its purpose
and its title since the original concept of the award was proposed in Resolution
No. 4 at the Grand Lodge 1979 Annual Communication, such resolution having
failed to pass beca}lse it was too restrictive on who was entitled to the award, its
limit of one award a year not taking into account a Lodge which may on occasion
wish to award more than one in a year; and
WHEREAS, the present understandingthat the award is the highest honor
that can be bestowed upon a brother by his Masonic Lodge is not proper as the
highest honor that can be bestowed on a Mason is the lambskin apron he received
in his First Degree.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that a new Section 23155 of
the California Masonic Code be added to read as follows:
§23155. HIRAM AW ARDS.

The Grand Lodge. ypon request of a Masonic Lodge under its
jyrjsdiction. shall furnish a certificate honoring the Master Mason
designated by the Lodge as a recipient of the Hiram Award. The
certificate shall be delivered to the Masonic Lodge for presentation to the
recipient. The Grand Lodge shall make available for purchase a
medallion and lapel pin for recipients of the Hiram Award.

266

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Lodge may only designate for the Hiram Award a Master Mason who
has served the Lodge and the Masonic Fraternity with devotion over anQ.
above the ordinary. Service as an officer or as Master of a Lodge shall
not be in itself sufficient gualification for the award nor shall it be a
disgualification. The award should be based on what the recipient has
done. not what positions he has held.
The Hiram Award shall be considered the highest honor for service that
can be bestowed upon a member by a Masonic Lodge. The presentation
should be made with appropriate ceremony. When a selection has been
made. it should be announced so the recipient may invite family and
friends to the award presentation. To maintain the prestige and
importance of the Hiram Award. a Lodge may present only one Hiram
Award in any one calendar year. Such limitation should not suggest that
this award should be presented every year.

§15050. ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES.
Alcoholic beverages may be sold, served, and consumed on property
owned by or leased to a Masonic Lodge, Temple Association, or Masonic
Organization and at Masonic activities held elsewhere if the following
requirements are observed:
A.

Alcoholic beverages may not be sold, served, or consumed in a
Lodge room or in a room in which Masonic ceremonies are
normally conducted except when such room serves a dual
purpose as a ceremonial room and social room;

B.

A Masonic Lodge, Temple Association, or Masonic
Organization may not maintain, on a regular or permanent basis,
a bar stocked with alcoholic beverages;

C.

Th.e funds of a Masonic Lodge or Temple Association may not
be used to purchase alcoholic beverages;

D.

Alcoholic beverages may not be served, consumed, or sold
during the course of a meeting of a Masonic Lodge, Temple
Association, or Masonic Organization;

E.

Except as provided at the end of this Section. a -IT Masonic
Lodge or Temple Association may not directly or indirectly
apply for, assume title to, or operate under any government
license or permit for the purpose of consuming, serving or
selling alcoholic beverages, whether in, on, or away from
premises owned, leased, or rented by either of them;

F.

A Masonic Lodge, Temple Association, or Masonic
Organization may not rent or lease property in which it has an
ownership interest to business establishments wherein alcoholic

consumption, and sale are incident to and not the primary

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit a Masonic Lodge or
Temple Association to hold a single event liquor license. Since the change in
Grand Lodge policy and law in 1989 so as to permit the sale, use, etc. of alcoholic
beverages to Masons at certain places and under certain conditions, it has been the
consistent policy of Grand Lodge to deny the mantle or aura or appearance of
ownership of either the product (alcoholic beverages) or the right to sell (the
license) to a Masonic Lodge or to a Masonic Temple Association . The Lodge
and/or Temple Association has been denied the right to own or store alcoholic
beverages, they cannot own or maintain a bar, and the funds of a Masonic Lodge
or Temple Association may not be used to purchase alcoholic beverages.
Permitting Lodges or Temple Associations to hold single event liquor
licenses is a substantial change in direction from the previous Grand Lodge
position, and is not consistent with current Grand Lodge policy.
Report ofthe Committee on Temple Properties and Taxation:

Although your Temple Properties and Taxation Committee sees the
possibility of financial advantages to this Resolution, we feel there are peripheral
ramifications; such as, the Unrah Act and American Disabilities Act Requirements
which are beyond the scope of this committee'smission statement. Therefore, we
feel that we cannot make a recommendation regarding this Resolution.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

Admissions Committee
by Victor Howard, Ph.D., and Ernest A. Poo/eon, Co-Chairmen
The Admissions Review Program of the Board is a carefully developed
analysis and evaluation process that, over the years, has been improved and refined
to meet the needs of our Homes Staff as well as our Applicants and the Board
itself.
Prior to the full Board Meeting, on the first Wednesday of each month, the
.
six Trustees who fonn the Admissions Committee, three from the North and three
from the South, have received and carefully studied the applications for Masonic
assistance. These Trustees review and evaluate the applications and then submit
their comments and votes to the two co-chainnen. The co-chainnen then discuss
the results of the vote by phone, and where significant differences occur, meetings
of the entire committee are arranged to take place prior to the regular Board
Meeting, at which time Homes StaffRepresentativesand Administratorsattend and
assist in the discussion.
Over the past several years experience has indicated that an overnight visit
to one of the facilities by all applicants is essential in order that Administrators and
Medical Staff can evaluate them and assist in detennining the most appropriate
placement. (The facility visited is not an indication of where the most appropriate

The number of applications handled by the committee for couples,
individuals and children varies from month to month. This past year the high was
nine applications handled in one month for seniors, and three applications in one
month for children.
Because of the continuing need to control admissions due to the ongoing
reconstruction at the Union City facility, and because the Skilled Nursing Facility
was operating close to maximum capacity, admissions during this year continued
to be restricted to those classified as "Independent Ambulatory". And, as was
anticipated, this continues to result in an increase in the number of persons
receiving Nonresident Assistance (NRA).
Paralleling this ongoing reduction at Union City, the adult section of
Covina continues to operate at maximum capacity. During the year, with the
guidance of our Medical Advisory Committee, in addition to converting one of our
buildings into an Assisted Living Facility, we were able to move ahead with the
modification of another senior resident building for this purpose as the need
continues to grow. ·Additionally, the necessary nursing and support personnel were
added to the staff. This allows most of our residents to remain in their Home at
Covina despite chronic health problems.
The co-chainnen gratefully acknowledge the hard work and dedication of
the Trustees who are on the Admissions Committee. The members are Thomas F.
Joy, Melville H. Nahin, Charles H. Alexander and Robert Peters. We also
acknowledge the work of the two Administrators, Kelly Wiest and Dale Ankney
and their staff.

by Jeff H. Eichner, Jr., Chairman
The Centennial Celebration Committee is charged with planning events
and activities during 1998 to celebrate the 100-year history of the Masonic Homes.
The committee presently includes eight members: Roy J. Henville, Stanley M.
Cazneaux, Anthony P. Wordlow, Alvin J. Weis, W. Bruce Pruitt, Kelly Wiest,
Dale Ankney and Jeff H. Eichner, Jr.
The theme for the centennial is "BUILDING A FUTURE UPON A
CENTURY OF CARING". In carrying out this theme, events and activities are

planned with the following goals: (I) Celebrate the first I 00 years of the Masonic
Homes of California; (2) Generate support for the second century of providing
facilities and care to the elderly and needy children; and (3) Strengthen rapport and
increase awareness of the Homes' facilities, services, and programs with California
Freemasons, their families, and the general public.

The first of the buildings, Wollenberg, was completed in January, 1997
and it is now occupied by some 28 residents who are very pleased with the
modernization. They and all residents are also enjoying and greatly benefitting
from the new Grider Health Center which is part of Wollenberg and affords a
therapeutic swimming pool and extensive therapy and exercise equipment.

A Centennial logo has been designed and preliminary work has been done
on a special publication commemorating the Homes' past, present and future.
Other planned activities and events include: a rededication and "open house" at
Union City and an evening commemorative event that includes entertainmentat the
California Masonic Memorial Temple on Saturday, October IO, 1998; a
rededication at Covina; displays of the Homes' evolution at Union City, Covina
and San Francisco during the centennial year; articles about the Homes in each
edition of the California Freemason during the centennial year; speaker/video
programs on the history and future of the Masonic Homes for lodges and other
interested groups; and special events for the residents at Union City and Covina.

The second building to be completely renovated is the Adams Building
where work started in December, 1996 and it should be completed in December,
1997 with occupancy by 38 residents shortly thereafter. Architectural work on the
next building, the North Wing, is almost finished and construction cost estimate
will be made shortly with work expected to commence in January, 1998.
Preliminary plans are in progress for the final two buildings, the Administration
and South Wings, in order to assure the continuity of architectural and construction
phases.

Most of the planning is complete for the 68th Annual Conference of the
Masonic Homes Executives' Association of North America that will be hosted by
the Masonic Homes of California, June 19-24, 1998. In addition to arranging for
meeting space and guest rooms at a hotel and identifying topics and potential
speakers, family tours and activities have been planned. Invitations and publicity
for the California Conference were handed out to participants at the Association's
Conference that was held in Minnesota in June, 1997.

Facility Services Committee
by Warren T. Buschmann, Chairman
The full Board of Trustees adopted a plan to initiate a major long-term
project ofrenovatingand retrofitting the five major buildings at Union City. Some
of these were constructed in the I 920's. In-depth studies fostered the proposal to
completely demolish the buildings' interiors leaving exteriors and structural steel
intact. This plan saved millions of dollars at each building while still making it
possible to enlarge resident room size to meet modem standards, upgrade seismic
strengths to meet today's technical knowledge, and at the same time update all
buildings to greatly enhance the quality of life for our residents. All buildings will
be supplied with heating and air conditioning from a central location,
communications of all types are improved including a telephone in each resident's
room. Many behind the scenes improvements were also made at the same time
such as lead and asbestos removal, new elevators, improved lighting, TV reception,
etc.

The year also saw the completion of the sixty year old swimming pool at
Covina which is now used by the adult residents as well as the children.
The above describes Board approved projects which the Facility
Committee oversees. In addition, the committee annually reviews, approves and
oversees numerous necessary and important projects at both Union City and
Covina in order that our physical plants may be kept up-to-date and smoothly
functioning.
The Facility Committee is made up of two additional members, namely
Tom Joy and Al Weis. Their very helpful comments and counsel is gratefully
acknowledged. Also, the accomplishments listed in this report would not have
been nearly as successful and possible without the dedicated and long-term efforts
of the previous Chairman of this Committee, Bill Dickson, and his contribution is
gratefully acknowledged.

Long Range Planning Committee
by Fred Sorsabal, Chairman
Seeing that a future plan of action was necessary to guide the Masonic
Homes of California into the next millennium, President Roy J. Henville, PGM,
appointed a committee to provide recommendations to the Masonic Homes Board
of Trustees to begin that process. The committee consisted of Fred Sorsabal,
Chairman; Bob Peters, Secretary; Melville H. Nahin, Senior Grand Warden;
Douglas A. Scott; Kelly Wiest, Administrator, Union City; and Dale Ankney,
Administrator, Covina.
It is the Board's responsibility to set the broad parameters by which the
Masonic Homes organization operates and to establish policies to guide the
implementation of those directives. Planning is a natural function of the Board's
responsibilities. The overall plan, therefore, will be the basis for many other Board
functions; for establishing priorities for the resources available; for continually
reviewing programs and services; for monitoring the progress in achieving goals;
and for providing an unequaled quality of service to our needy Brethren and their
families. The Plan must remain flexible and under periodic review due to the rapid
rate of change occurring within the Health Care industry, it's regulatory bodies and
society's ever-pressing priority to satisfy the long-term care needs of it's seniors
and children. Because of the need for an annual review of the Plan, the Board of
Trustees has established the Long Range Planning Committee as a permanent
committee to assist it in keeping abreast of the changes so that the Board of
Trustees can respond thoughtfully and appropriately as the need arises.
In as much as the full report is on file with the Grand Secretary, the
remainder of this report will consist of the recommendations to the Board of
Trustees:

l.

2.

Children's Home: It was recommended and adopted by the
Board of Trustees to approve the concept of admitting a limited
larger number of"non-masonic" children to the Home at Covina
outside of the current P.A.L. program and to request that the
Grand Master be asked to submit a Grand Master's
Recommendation at the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge
approving this change in procedure of admissions.
It was recommended and adopted by the Board of Trustees to
accept and approve the concept of construction of a new
"duplex" cottage on the site of one of the existing cottages as a
"pilot project" to see if it will more nearly meet the needs of the
"Family Home Model" of care that has been recently
implemented at the Covina Home for Children.

Planned Giving Program
by Jeff H. Eichner, Jr., Director ofCharitable Giving
The Planned Giving Program is charged with the responsibility of
providing information and assistance to people on how to make gifts to the
Masonic Homes. During the year assistance was provided to individuals, fmanc ial
advisors and attorneys in various ways to make charitable gifts.

Throughout this period, the Board and the two Homes Administrators
relied upon our Director of Human Resources, Dawn Graeff, for a high level of
guidance and support.
Among the other priority efforts completed by this committee and the staff
was the annual review of comparative compensation and benefits information for
all job classifications. As a result of the annual benefit survey analysis, certain
modifications to existing programs were made that provide cost savings as well as
greater benefits to our employees.
In addition, with the assistance of our Director of Human Resources, this
committee has maintained on-going oversight of issues relating to discipline, of
communication to reduce liability and improve employee relations, as well as ongoing oversight of Workers Compensation issues to reduce liability and contain
costs.

I would like to acknowledge the dedication and cooperation of committee
members Frederick L. Sorsabal and Charles H. Alexander, and the very capable
assistance of Union City Administrator, Kelly Wiest, and Covina Administrator,
Dale Ankney, as well as the continuing support of our Director of Human
Resources, Dawn Graeff.

Some of the Planned Giving Program options provide attractive and viable
ways for donors to receive a lifetime income, receive and income tax deduction,
and avoid capital gains tax while supporting the Masonic Homes. These options
include the Pooled Income Fund and charitable remainder trusts.
The Pooled Income Fund offers an easy way to make a charitable gift to
the Masonic Homes and receive a lifetime income from the gift and receive tax
breaks. During the year $I 03,000 was added to existing accounts, six new
accounts were established for $75,000, and $5,000 was transferred to the Masonic
Homes. As of June 30, 1997, the Pooled Income Fund had 71 participants (up
9.1%) with a year-end principal of $4.76 million.
During the year information and assistance was provided to many
individuals establishing charitable remainder trusts that benefit the donor as well
as the Masonic Homes. In these cases, the donors receive a lifetime income based
on the full value of their gifts, avoid capital gains tax, if applicable, and take a
charitable tax deduction for up to six years.
Bequests are one of the most common methods of making gifts to the
Masonic Homes and information on wills and bequests was disseminated
throughout the year. The Totten Trust is used also to designate the Masonic
Homes as the beneficiary of an individual's savings account(s) in banks and other
savings institutions. The money in the savings account belongs to the donor who
can withdraw it at any time with the balance of the account going to the Masonic
Homes at the time of the donor's death.
Charitable giving through a living trust is another popular method of
giving to the Masonic Homes and information and assistance was provided upon
request during the year. The advantagesofrevocable and irrevocable living trusts
include reducing or eliminating estate taxes, maintaining control of an estate even
during disability, control over distribution of assets, and avoiding lengthy and
costly probate. Such trusts can be used to achieve both charitable and
noncharitable objectives that can benefit the individual, family members, and the
Masonic Homes.

Real Estate Committee
by Robert D. Peters, Chairman
The Real Estate Committee of the Masonic Homes of California is
charged with the responsibility of disposing of all real estate made available to the
Masonic Homes through asset assignment, wills and bequests, gifts and grants.
During the past year, July 1, 1996 through June 30, 1997, we sold sixteen
(16) pieces of property for a total of$586, 150, and sixteen (16) motor vehicles for
a total of $57,324. Total sales for 1996/97 equal $643,474. In addition, net
reductions in our "Notes Receivable" were $450,391.65. We continue to carry
thirty-one (31) notes on property sold, with a total value of$1,256,009.47.
We always have an inventory of unsold properties, due to the Life Care
Contract signed by each new resident of the Home. This affords them a ninety (90)
day period to adjust and satisfy in their own minds that they have no intention of
withdrawing from the Masonic Home. The resident then signs a release
authorizing the sale of the property.
At the end of 1996, Brother Hambleton Leas, fonner President of the
Board of Trustees, then serving as the Real Estate Coordinator for the Homes,
announced that he wished to retire. Brother Tom McKinney was recommended to
the Board as his replacement, and both of these fine brethren have been working
together over the past several months towards a smooth transition of this very
important post. The Board thanks Brother Leas for his many years of wise counsel
and wishes him well in his retirement.

perhaps "borderline", (GPA 1.6) but he assures us that his grade point

Report of the Adminis trator
Masonic Home, Union City
1996-1997
"Those who decide to use leisure as a means of mental development, who
love good music, good books, good pictures, good plans, good company,
good conversa tion-wha t are they? They are the happiest people in the
world."
--William Lyon Phelps
As Administ ratorof our great home at Union City, I am pleased to infonn
you through this annual report that most of our residents fit the above quotation!
However, I would propose one addition to the above quote which would be "good
exercise" through the New Grider Center. Since it's opening in the first quarter of
I 997, many of our residents have found that regular exercise, either by using the
new 1,321 sq. ft exercise center or doing water aerobics in the Grider 19' x 39'
heated indoor pool, not only makes them happy, but maintains their good health for
a longer time! Especially, happy are the residents who moved into the new
Wollenberg residence which was dedicated by Grand Master Allen B. Gresham on
December 16, I 996.
The Adams Building is our current residence under renovation and
earthquake retrofitting. When completed in early 1998 there will be a total of 38
Assisted Living Apartments on the upper three floors: 13 on the fifth floor, 13 on
the fourth floor, and 12 on the third floor. There will be 31 single and seven
couple's apartments resembling the style of the Wollenberg Apartments, but with
smaller patio doors, more counter space, and pull cords rather than wands to open
and close draperies, private bathrooms, private telephones as well as other
improvements. The kitchen area and the size of the single apartments will be
similar to the Wollenberg Apartments, while the couple's apartments will be larger.
A Laundry Room will be located on the fourth floor. These improvements were
greatly needed as the original apartments had residents sharing a small bathroom
and using a central bath/shower room.
The second floor of Adams will house our large and well known ceramics
program, Channel 3 (our in-house television station), a new Computer Learning
Center wired for the Internet, a large living room, a kitchen for cooking classes and
dining area for parties, Recreation staff offices, restrooms, and crafts, sewing, and
painting areas. In addition, the entrance door near the Siminoff Center will have
an electric sliding door.
The buildings to be renovated next and brought up to the latest earthquake
building codes will be (in order) the North Wing, Main Administrative Building,
and the South Wing. This work will take place between 1998 and 2000. Living

space in the single apartments in these buildings average approximately 220 sq. ft.
When renovated the average single apartments will be approximately 450 sq. ft.

fruit trees and will provide a secure walking/seating area for our dementia
residents. An outdoor emergency pull cord system is also being installed for
ultimate resident safety. As our residents use this sunny, fresh air area, we feel
certain that their quality of life will be enhanced.
All capital improvements are made for the benefit of our current and
future residents. Our population census indicates that as of June 30, 1997, we had
235 residents, with 59 Masons and 176 spouses. There were 23 couples.
The average age of our residents is 87. This year, several Covina
residents who required Skilled Nursing Care were transferred to our Home. Their
names and Lodges appear in our resident population report. The Home is proud
to share the names of the following centenarians within it's population:

Masonic Homes Benefit

We are always grateful for the many Masonic affiliated groups who have
helped the Home for a variety of reasons. During the past year there were 28
Masonic Lodge visits, 14 Eastern Star Chapter visits, 23 assemblies of Rainbow
Girls, 4 Bethel of Jobs Daughters, and 4 Chapter of DeMolay visits.
The Home's employees continue to provide excellent health care to our
sisters and brothers. This was documented by the California Department of Health
Services last September when the Department visited for their annual survey.
Shirley Weber, Associate Administrator and Carmen Nicholson, our Director of
Nursing Services and all of our Lorber Skilled Nursing employees are to be
commended for receiving an excellent Survey!
In March of 1997, Bhupinder Bhandari, M.D. and Associates were
engaged as primary care physicians for our residents. Dr. Bhandari ensures

continuity of care and also follows our residents when their health status requires
transfers to local hospitals.
Dr. John Rashkis came aboard as our new Medical Director in August of
1997. His excellent medical credentials and experience as Medical Director in
other Long Term Care facilities will provide guidance to us as we continue to
improve the health care we offer.

In 1998, the Masonic Homes of California will celebrate it's centennial
year. Our year long theme will be "Building a Future Upon a Century of Caring."
What an appropriate theme for a fraternity that truly does care about its members!
A rededication is planned on October 12, 1998 and in June of 1998, Masonic
Homes of California will host the annual meeting of the Masonic Homes
Executives Association of North America as well as many other events which are
still in the planning stage.
Once again, it is impossible to provide you with a day-to-day report about
the numerous great things that occur at this magnificent home. The intent of this
report is to provide you with some of the highlights of what life is like at the Union
City facility. Whenever you are in the area, please stop and tour your Masonic
Home and see, first hand, the great things which your Masonic contributions help
support.
A very special recognition to the members of the Endowment Board for
efforts in obtaining funds to support all efforts at Union City and

and sincere dedication of all employees who provide daily care to our residents and

Report of the Administrator
Masonic Homes, Covina
1996-1997
As I reported to the fraternity in my previous Annual Report, the 1995/96
year was a year of transition for our Home in Covina which challenged our care
givers to professionalize their skills to meet the needs of our changing senior and
children clientele. This year I am happy to report to you that our staff met that
challenge and, as a result, our residents now receive care appropriate to both their
physical and psychological needs.

July 1, 1996- June 30, 1997

Not only have we employed professional health care staff in our adult
community to provide quality care to our residents, 24 hours a day, seven days a
week, but we have also completely retrained our child care staff. Through a
consulting relationship with the Boys Town organization, perhaps the leader in
providing residential treatment to adolescents, our staff has been trained in
advanced child care techniques that ultimately will lead to their achieving
professional certified status.
In the following report I will explain to you some of the changes made at
Covina and the resulting benefits of those changes. And although we are proud we
have met with great accomplishmentthis past year, we are even more excited about
our future. I hope you share in our enthusiasm as I relate to you our
accomplishments over the past year.
During 1996/97 our Assisted Living community on the adult side of our
campus reached new heights in its service to our residents. To understand why the
demands for this level of care have increased, it would be prudent to define what
assisted living care is. Assisted living care is an intermediate level of care between
independent living and skilled nursing care. Its purpose is to provide care to those
seniors who are in need of moderate to heavy assistance in their activities of daily
living such as bathing, dressing and ambulating. In addition, such residents require
assistance in the administration of their medications that the Home centrally stores
for the resident's own safety.
Given the advanced age of the typical adult resident at Covina, one can
see that it was in the best interests of the facility and our residents to offer an
assisted living service. By expanding our services, our organization benefits from
reduced expenditures associated with outplacement. More importantly however,
our residents are provided with the opportunity to remain in their homes as long as
possible before their health condition requires transfer elsewhere. This philosophy
of care is in keeping with trends found outside the Masonic Home where medical
care is increasingly being provided in a home setting.

312

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Although assisted living care was introduced at Covina during the latter
part of the previous fiscal year, it was this past year in which it reached its pinnacle
of success. By the end of the 1996/97 year, fifty-six residents had received care
in our assisted living setting. Today, seventeen residents call the Ashwood
Building their home (our assisted living facility). Without this new service, these
seventeen residents would have to be outplaced in local contract facilities in the
Southern California area, or would be required to transfer to our facility located at
Union City. And although this latter option would serve our residents medical
needs better than any other facility of its kind in America, the transfer may be
emotionally traumatizing and most definitely would remove many residents from
the close proximity of their family members who reside in Southern California.
We are very proud of the establishment of our new assisted living
community at Covina, but we're not resting upon our accomplishments as we
embark upon the future. The next step Covina is taking to improve health care
delivery to its residents is to establish hospice care services right on our own
campus. Hospice care is defined as an interdisciplinary program of palliative care
and supportive services that address physical, spiritual, social and economic needs
oftenninally ill patients and their families.

known as house parents) have been trained to function not only as role models for
the youth in their charge, but to provide guidance in those matters specific to a
child's individualized needs.

Effective January I, 1997, regulations within the State of California were
revised, pennittingResidential Care Facilities of the Elderly (RCFE) to provide onsite hospice services to their residents. In order to do so, an RCFE must employ
properly trained licensed medical staff and contract with a licensed hospice care
provider to administer a fonnalized program of hospice care.
Anticipating a change in regulations, the health care management team at
Covina hired the appropriately credentialed staff and negotiated a care agreement
with one of the most outstanding hospice care providers in the Southern California
area, East San Gabriel Hospice. We are now in the process of filing the necessary
paperwork with the State to establish hospice care at Covina, and we finnly believe
approval from the State will be granted by the end of the current year. When
granted, Covina is in a position to provide its residents hospice care immediately.
Not to be outdone by the Adult Services Department, our Child Care
Services Department underwent its dramatic change since the early l 970's when
the old donnitory buildings were razed and the new group homes built in their
place. Although bricks and mortar did not change this time, the revisions to the
child care program were no less dramatic.
With the guidanceofthe Boys Town organization, the Children's Home
at Covina implemented the Family Home Model of Care, a decentralized approach
to child care not unlike the kind of care a child would receive in a nonnal family
setting. Through an exhaustive training program, our Family Specialists ( fonnerly

313

Unlike twenty-five years ago, the youth in our Home today are unlikely
to be in placement solely because they are orphans. Today's youth resident is more
likely to have come to us because his home environment was unsuitable for his
continued residency. For example, the child may have been subjected to physical
or emotional abuse that necessitated his removal from harm's way. Or, the child
may have been the victim of a disease such as attention deficit disorder or
hyperactivity disorder, which resulted from his parent's substance abuse during
pregnancy and which now manifests itself in behaviors the parents are unable to
manage. Thus, the model of care appropriate to children who were residents of the
home just two decades ago is not appropriate for the children of today who come
to us with a host of psychological disorders.
The training of our Family Specialists at present is not complete, but the
results of that training thus far have already been dramatic. In general, the school
grades of the Home's children have consistently improved since implementation
of the Family Home Model of Care. Perhaps more importantly, our children are
beginning to understand that their lives have meaning and that a rewarding life
awaits them if they become more focused in their approach to life. It will be an
additional mark of success when our staff builds upon its existing record of
accomplishment ~y assisting our children to reach their maximum potentials.
During the coming year, the challenge to our child care staff will be to
reach the "Certified" credential status, which is the final step in their professional
development following their training in the Family Home Model of Care. This
certification will be evidence that our Family Specialists have met the highest
standards in professional child care, and will be further evidence of the fact our
children are receiving the best possible care.
Simply completing two and one-halfyears of training will not result in our
Family Specialists earning their certifications. Each Family Specialist must first
undergo a thorough assessment by our consultants from Boys Town. This
assessment is not unlike audits to which the most sophisticated businesses find
themselves subject, and this rigorous assessment is not a once in a lifetime
experience. In order to maintain their certification credential, the Family
Specialists will be subject to additional assessments each ensuing year. Future
assessments will not only include a re-evaluation of the employee's fundamental
training, but it will assess how well he or she has employed the use of new care
techniques taught during the most recent year. As can be seen, our new child care
program is indeed rigorous, but one which our children truly deserve and need.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Our past year was definitely a year of accomplishment and one in which
all of our residents benefitted from the hard work of a very loving staff. It is a staff
that all of us within the Fraternity can be proud. On behalf of the Covina staff, I
would like to thank all of my fellow Brothers and their families for the support you
have given the Covina Home over the past year. Your words of encouragement
and participation in activities at our Home are more meaningful than you could
ever imagine. As we enter this new year of challenges and opportunities, we look

Children Residents

forward to your input and participation in our many Home events. Covina is your
Home, and one in which all of us can take pride. We look forward to seeing many
of you at the Covina Home during the coming year.

Respectfully submitted,
Dale Ankney, Administrator

President's Report
by Roy J. Henvi//e, PGM
From California Masonic History we learn that Friday, October 14, 1892,
the Masonic Homes of California was declared to be an Institution! The
membership of the jurisdiction then was 16,000 with 50 lodges. At that Annual
Communication of Grand Lodge, the first annual report of the Board of Trustees
reported that lodges and other contributors had pledged to the Masonic Widows'
and Orphans' Home upwards of$45,000.

This is the 1051h Annual Report of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic
Homes of California.
From the time the first Board of Trustees was appointed and the Home
was completed was a period of six years. The dedication took place on October 12,
1898. Next year will be the centennial year of the Masonic Homes. A committee

320

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of the Board of Trustees has been at work planning for a celebration of the
wonderful accomplishments of 100 years of activities at the Home.

supervision and training of the children could be increased to accommodate the
added number. So far as budget is concerned, 51 children in the past was not a
problem nor would it be at the present time. The Board of Trustees, along with the
Administrative Staff, have studied this matter at great length. As a result, we have
requested the Grand Master to recommend a change in the rules of admission. The
plan would permit children that have no known Masonic relationship to be
admitted. All other rules would remain unchanged. Children would continue to
be sponsored by a lodge and are usually admitted between the ages of 5 and 15
years of age. Masonic related children would always be admitted or have a priority
to non-related children. In the Masonic Homes Executive Association, there are
6 jurisdictions that have Homes for children. None of them, except California,
require a Masonic relationship to be admitted.
We hope that sharing existing facilities and assistance with a limited
number of additional children that are in need, will meet with your approval.
The annual report of the Masonic Homes operations are available. We
hope you will avail yourself of this valuable information.

Construction of the first building commenced in 1896. True to the
statementthat "Masonsare Builders'',constructionhas continued to this very day.
Two years ago, you will recall, we embarked on a plan to completely
rebuild and modernize five of the main buildings at Union City. This proram
proceeds in an orderly manner of one building at a time to minimize the
disturbance to our residents. The second of these buildings will be completed
before the year end.
The first building completed, the Wollenberg building, on one floor has
an innovative health center. This includes exercise equipment and a therapy pool
which has proven to be very beneficial. With the age of our residents ranging from
75 to over 100 years of age, the use of canes, walkers, and even wheelchairs are an
aid to mobility. With the activities in the health center, many are beginning to
discard these aids. Aches and pains from arthritis is diminishing. There is no
question, people are living longer these days. We believe that through use of the
health center, our residents will be more active and enjoy better health in their
advancing years.
Another ignoration recently completed is an enclosed outside walking
garden area for those with a dementia problem. For their health benefit, outside
fresh air walking exercise in an area of benches, plants, an aviary and pets is highly
recommended. With this kind of activity it is hoped the dementia will not increase
and better health will occur.
We have modified one of the rules of admission for adults at the Home.
A long standing rule has required each individual to be ambulatory at the time of
admission. Now, in the application of couples, the change will permit them to be
admitted even if one may require "Assisted Living Care". This will open the door
for couples who have been confronted with such a problem.
The Home at Covina was established in 1915, exclusively for children.
Through the years, the Covina Home has touched the lives of more than 1,800
children. In 1990, 56 apartments were opened for adults. Today the population at
Covina consists of 22 children and 63 adults. Nearly all of the apartments are
occupied. The children's current quarters were built in 1970. Instead of the
dormitory style buildings prior to that time, their facilities now consist of 10
cottages, housing 8 children per unit.
In 1985, the enrollment was 51 children of which 21 were high school
students. The number has declined to less than half of that number in just 12 years.
For the purpose of efficiency, approximately 50 children would be an ideal
number. The facilities are more than adequate for that number. The staff for care,

On behalf of the Board of Trustees and the offices at San Francisco and
Covina, we wish to thank all who have served on investigating committees or have
assisted in the application process for Masonic Assistance.
Of a personal note, I wish to express my sincere thanks for the honor and
privilege of serving on the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees for the past nine
years.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF THE

Every effort is being made to convince the members of this Grand Lodge
of the importance ifmaintaining'the health and vitality of the Endowment Fund.
About one-third of the support for the operations of the Homes is represented by
income from that fund. It is only by continued growth of the fund that the Homes
can continue to offer our needy brethren and sweethearts the loving care they
deserve. As most of you will know, we are now giving public recognition in the
California Freemason magazine to those brethren who are major contributors to
the Endowment Fund. We believe that such recognition, which is a very common
procedure among most charities, will be the best way to demonstrate how much the
Homes appreciates those brethren who participate well above the average.

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers and Members of the Grand
Lodge, Brethren: I am pleased to report to you on the successful fund raising
campaign which was held during the 1996-1997 fiscal year. The membership of
our Grand Lodge continues to decrease, but the contributions made by those
dedicated brothers who are still supportive of our Masonic Homes remain at an
encouraging level.
The total contributions from the brethren, through the individual lodges,
amounted to $1,023,916.75. This represents a decrease of$88,679.06 from the
total contributions last year. The overall average per member amounted to $9.73,
also a decrease from the average of$10.l l last year. The encouraging aspect is
that, although only 35% of our membership saw fit to make any contribution at all,
those brothers who did so made an average contributionof$28.09, an increase over
the average of $25.30 for last year.
Of the 423 lodges which comprise the Grand Lodge ofCalif~rnia, 151
achieved the Honor Roll with the required average contributions of$10.70.
Total gifts to the Endowment Fund were as follows:
Wills & Bequests . . . . . . . . . . . . $3,255,016,17
Contributions through Lodges . . . 1,023,916.24
Undesignated contributions . . . . . . . . 15,004.24
Memorial contributions ............ 7,660.00
Total Gifts ................. $4,301,597.16
It is important to note how significant the wills and bequests are to the
health of our Endowment Fund. For this reason I sincerely trust that every one of
the Worshipful Masters in this room will return to their Lodges and give a strong
reminder to the brethren that they should not forget the Homes when they prepare
their wills.

Your Endowment Board is ready and willing to assist you in a number of
ways to improve your fund raising efforts for this important cause. We are anxious
to visit your Lodge and tell the brethren and ladies about what is going on at the
Homes and about the great purpose for which your contributions are being used.
The history book, "The Greatest of These is Charity", will be presented to each of
your newly initiated Entered Apprentices, if you will ensure your board member
receives copies of your trestleboard.

You have heard in the report from the Board of Trustees about the major
improvements which have been made to the physical plant. You have also heard
about the enhanced programs in assisted living and youth care. All of the Trustees
and staff directly associated with the Homes work very heard to represent us well
in the care for our children and elderly. We need to do our part by making an
annual contribution to the Endowment Fund.
The year 1998 represents the 1OOth Anniversary of our Masonic Homes.
Several special events will take place during the year to recognize that significant
milestone. Won'teach of you pledge right now to make a special effort to be a part
of that celebration? Take your Lodge and visit one or both of the Homes. Make
a visitation and confer a degree. There will be a roll of labels showing the
centennial logo in eyery Lodge package. Use those labels, and get more from me
if needed. I urge you, in the strongest way, to make this fiscal year the year that
the giving to the Homes turns around. Let's show the world that we really do care
about those brothers, wives, and children to who we have promised: "We will take
care of you!"
Respectfully submitted,
W. Bruce Pruitt, Chairman

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.Ma/California:
Most Worshipful, Grand Lodge Officers, Past Grand Masters, Past Grand
Officers, Distinguished Guests, Members of the Grand Lodge, Visitors and My
Brethren.
To serve as President of the Board of Trustees of the California Masonic
Foundation is both an honor and a privilege, and I thank the Trustees for their
confidence in electing me to that office.
We have continued to remain focused on the Foundation's mission; to
youth of our country as they strive to become productive citizens.
the
support
The Board continues to meet quarterly, at the Covina Home and at the
Grand Lodge office in a continuing effort to minimize administrative expenses.
M :. W :. William Stovall, PGM, continues to serve as a director on the
National Foundation for Children. Your Foundation was pleased to donate
$10,000 to assist in the expansion of the Masonic Student Assistance Program
throughout North America.
As in past years, the Foundation presented each of our four youth groups
with $2,500 for use in their leadership training programs.
CertificatesofRecognition and $1,000 checks were presented to each of
California's five "Teachers of the Year". This donation is to be used at their
discretion within their school districts. This affords our Grand Master and
members of the California Masonic Foundation and Public Schools Committee an
opportunity to discuss the Masonic Student Assistance Program and our
scholarship program with our State Board of Education.
In our continuing efforts to support public education, the Grand Master
presented $500 and a certificate to each school hosting a cornerstone ceremony.
This money is to be used at their discretion within the school.
Many students today would not be able to pursue a college education
without the aid of scholarship funds. I am pleased to report your Foundation
assisted 175 young adults in their pursuit of knowledge. Nine $10,000 awards
were presented to graduating high school seniors from a new fund in the name of
C.E. Towne. An additional fifty (50) $2,000 awards were presented at high school
award ceremonies. Two thousand dollar awards were also presented to 116
returning college students. The total value of this year's awards as $424,000.

The Masonic Student Assistance Program (MSAP) continues as a viable
part of our education program.

Today's actions are tomorrow's legacy. The future of our country, the
freedom of future generations, the legacy we hope to leave this world are expressed
in the Foundation's motto:

Since its inception in November, 1994, more than 586 educators from 273
schools and districts have been trained in this innovative approach to student
assistance. All classes for the 97-98 school year are full, as are several classes for
the 98-99 school year. Educators continue their praise of this program and of our
fraternity for recognizing the need for this type of training in our school system.
The BoardofTrustees of the California Masonic Foundation would like
to thank Dale Ankney and his staff at the Covina Home for their continued support
of our MSAP program. They are always ready to assist the Foundation staff and
guest educators when on campus. Their dedication to this program enables us to
host nine (9) classes yearly.
To date, over 5,000 children have been referred to core teams in
California. My Brethren, that's 5,000 cries for help that have been answered;
5,000 children that will be better citizens tomorrow because the Masons cared
about them today.
A new video on MSAP will be released shortly to all Lodges, Past Grand
Masters, the Public Schools Committee, the Executive Committee and Foundation
Board members. It is hoped you will avail yourself of the opportunity to show it
in your Lodges.
The Public Schools Committee continued its support of the Foundation
by acting as the liaison between Lodges and schools with teams in their area.
Several Public Schools members have attended MSAP training and have a better
understanding of the process and its value to educators.
By working together, with our Lodges assisting the schools with materials
needed by the teams, and with the MSAP core teams identifying and helping
children in pain, we will make our state a better place in which to live.
My Brethren, the lifeblood of our program is your financial support. We
currently sponsor programs for children from kindergarten through four years of
college. We presently offer a magnificent community service and we need to do
all in our power to cause this service to grow and come closer to meeting the needs
of our young people. The future of our country and the leaders of tomorrow will
be dependent upon the programs we provide.
It has been my extreme pleasure to serve as President of this Board and
I will miss working with the Board members.

I wish them continued success. May our programs grow and prosper
under their new President. May the California Masonic Foundation long remain
a viable link between the Masonic Fraternity and our communities.

Noe HILL MASONIC MANAGEMENT, INC.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

As President and on behalfofthe Board ofDirectorsofNob Hill Masonic
Management, Inc. {Nob Hill), I am pleased to present the fifth annual operating
report for this for-profit corporation, a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Grand
Lodge. Nob Hill was incorporated on February 7, 1992 and commenced
operations on May 1, 1992. It operates the California Masonic Memorial
auditorium, parking garage, exhibit hall and various rental properties under the
terms of an operating lease with the California Masonic Memorial Temple. This
report deals with the operations of Nob Hill for the fiscal year July 1, 1996 through
June 30, 1997.
This past year was a year of transition for Nob Hill's management and
operations, as we began a new phase in our life and development. As was reported
last year, our first General Manager retired as planned on March 31, 1997. Ray
Ward was the perfect start-up professional we needed to launch this major forprofit undertaking. Ray made an enormous contribution under the direction and
guidance of Most Worshipful Donald B. McCaw, Past Grand Master, founding
president and guiding force during the first five years of operation. My brethren,
Nob Hill has achieved all we expected and more under Don McCaw's leadership
and throughout Ray Ward's tenure. We owe them both a debt of gratitude and
appreciation. Especially to our Most Worshipful Brother Don who so generously
gave thousands of hours of uncompensated legal and administrative time in the
service of Nob Hill. It was this service and numerous other fraternal assignments,
past, present and future, that qualified our brother to be our Mason of the Year in
1994. We acknowledge again with this report that Brother Don's devotion and
dedication to service on our behalf continues even today, and without doubt into
many, many tomorrows. For now a simple "thank you" must suffice.
On March 1, 1997, James B. Willers was hired as the new Executive Vice
President/General Manager, after a nation-wide search and the evaluation and
review of dozens of qualified and experienced candidates. And on July 1, 1997,
Most Worshipfu!Don McCaw and I changed places for the balance of the Masonic
year. Don stayed on to complete the year as Vice President of the Board and will
continuethereafteras an advisor in connection with all legal matters related to the
Americans With Disabilities Act (ADA) lawsuits.
You will recall t~at last year we reported a Summons and Complaint filed
by two handicapped patrons of this auditorium who attended a Jazz In The City

331

For ease of understanding and ready comparison, this annual report will
follow the previously established practice of reporting the most significant and
important financial data.
As has been true every year since Nob Hill's formation we are pleased to
again report increased revenues and payment of rent this past year to the Temple
of $418,384 up from $388,458 last year. Since commencing operations five years
ago total rental payments of $1, 768,497 have been made to the Memorial Temple.
One of the most significant operating measurements for the auditorium
and exhibit hall is the number of event days. This past year we set a record of 253
event days as compared to 208 in 1995 and l 09 in the year before Nob Hill
commenced its management.
Although garage expenses were down net parking revenues were off
primarily due to the necessary and required accommodation for construction of the
library/museum. Additionally every garage on the hill reported revenue shortfall
this past year. Fortunately for us, this shortfall was more than off-set by increased
revenues from the auditorium and exhibit hall which were up 14%.
Overall our net income after taxes for the year ending June 30, 1997 was
$110,148 versus $145,718 the previous year which would indicate we earned less
money this year versus last. However, this year we increased rental payments to
the Temple by nearly $30,000.00 and enhanced the Pine Street Properties by over
$54,000.00. Accordingly at the July 1997 Board meeting a dividend of$50,000
payable October l st was declared making a total of $200,000 distributed to you,
our stockholders since we commenced operations.
My brethren, the dividend stream, the substantial rental payments to the
Temple and the conservative operating reserves all confirm the wisdom of
establishing Nob Hill. Operating performance continues to meet or exceed the
high hopes and expectations of Nob Hill's founders . And recognition for our
success must be given to the dedicated and devoted Nob Hill staff. They have
proven more than capable of carrying forward the legacy of this magnificent

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

This is the second year that this body is to consider a request for the
issuance of a Charter to a Lodge Under Dispensation.
The Dispensation to Black Mountain Lodge, U.D. was continued until
October I, 1997 at the recommendation of then Grand Master, Charles H.
Alexander, they having been instituted only one month previous to the 1996 Grand
Lodge Communication. They have now operated for a year and one month under
dispensation and are requesting a Charter at this Communication of Grand Lodge.
A member of the Charters Committee has worked with them during the year and
has examined their records and finds them to be in order. He also reports that they
have conferred three (3) First Degrees, two (2) Second Degrees and one ( 1) Third
Degree and have accepted one (I) affiliate member. They are active in the
community and have visited and were visited by the local Prince Hall Lodge. They
have complied with all the requirements of Grand Lodge and I therefore move that
a Charter be granted to Black Mountain Lodge and a number assigned by the
Grand Secretary.

Resolution No. 96-15, will be reported on at the appropriate time. Otherwise, the

The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the Grand
Master and the legal adviser to Grand Lodge when in session. The committee
reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to be considered at the next
Annual Communication and prepares any necessary legislation to carry out the
intent of the proponents. At the Annual Communication, it comments on the
legality of the Grand Master's decisions and dispensations and on the legal effect
of the proposed recommendations and resolutions.
After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code to reflect
the legislation which was adopted.
In the committee's view, those of Grand Master Gresham's decisions and
dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his discretion. In the
committee's view, the legislation mailed by the Grand Secretary on July 23rd of
this year is sufficient to carry out the intent of the proponents, and the legislation
contained in Grand Master Gresham's recommendations which he will present in
his message is sufficientto carry out his intent. We believe that each piece of this
legislation has the Ir.gal effect set forth in it.
The legislation mailed by the Grand Secretary on July 23rd of this year
and the legislation contained in Grand Master Gresham's recommendationsrequire
no separate motion because they are automatically before this Annual
Communication. The presiding officer will announce the vote required for passage
of each item before discussion begins. Any legislation which does not amend the
California Masonic Code or the Ritual requires a simple majority only for
adoption. Any amendment to the California Masonic Code or the Ritual must be
adopted by a five-sixths affirmative vote. If the amendment receives a simple
majority but less than a five-sixths affirmative vote, it carries over to the next
Annual Communication when only a two-thirds affirmative vote is required for
adoption.

Executive Secretaries
The Executive Secretaries of the 10 Service Bureaus who serve our
fraternity deserve special recognition for the long hours that are required to
perform the duties required of the office. The full spectrum of their duties cover
such items as: answering questions from the general public (about Masonry);
tracking down those Brethren that have lost touch with their home Lodge;
communicating with the member Lodges regarding Masonic funerals,
investigations and dissemination of information regarding charlatans who wish to
defraud a Masonic Lodge and tracking the financial condition of the respective
Bureau. To these Brethren, this Committee expresses its' deepest gratitude.
The following are some odds and ends about a few of those gentlemen
who have, or are, serving this fraternity.
Warren Carr of the Central Valley Bureau spent a good portion of this
year recovering from either knee replacement or heart by-pass surgery. The
members of that Bureau were quick to lend Bro. Carr assistance when needed.
Wor. Dave Patterson of the Los Angeles Masonic Service Bureau, held
the office of President of the Masonic Service Association of the United States.
Wor. Pattersons' duties, in addition to those normally expected of such an
auspicious office, included organizing bake sales, performing slight of hand tricks
for the sight impaired and helping lost puppies and kittens find their owners.
The Executive Secretary of the East Bay Masonic Service Bureau, Wor
Amie Ascerion, asked to be relieved of his duties as of October 31 , 1996 due to
failing health. Wor Ascerion was called to "that house not made with hands" in late
November 1996. All who knew this Mason were deeply saddened by his passing.
