Consolid ation of San Francisc o Area Bureaus
The consolidation of the East Bay, Southern Alameda and San Francisco
Bureaus occurred on Novembe r l , 1996. This consolidationhas met with resistance
from many of the Lodges in this area. The reasons for objection range from "not
providing services to the Lodges", to "the Service Bureau being too distant from
the constituent Lodge" The Lodges in the Richmond area have asked to fonn their
own Bureau, but that was denied at the time as the ongoing consolidation had not
had time to prove or disprove its' worthiness. This Committee infonned the
petitioning Lodges that discussion of this issue could be reopened at a later date.

REPOR T OF THE COMM ITTEE
ON MEMO RIAL SERVIC E
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Grand Lodge Officers, Past and Former Grand
Lodge Officers, Brethren:
On behalf of the members of your Memorial Service Committee,
Worshipful Brothers Robert N. Deter and William N. Wine, former Grand
Chaplains Emile R. Laversin and Alexander H. Swan, and our Grand Chaplain,
the
Very Reverend David R. Doan:
We have come to share a moment of sacred memory in recogntion of
those who have ended their earthly pilgrimage and completed their quest for that
ultimate light which shines in the lives of all men everywhere but particula
rly
within those who recognize the great I AM as the Creator and Lord of us all.
As Brother Master Masons, we come to do homage to these, our departed
brethren, who have arrived at the place where dwells that house not made with
hands eternal in the heavens . We can never do justice in recognition to their work
nor their completed service, nor can we express enough gratitude to them for
the
paths that they have blazed upon the ashes of those of our brethren who have gone
before them nor for the building of the fraternity which they have assisted
in
erecting.
Their work is completed. High Twelve has come and they ahve gone
from labor to refreshment. The trowel is set aside but their works do follow them
and for this, we too, give our prayer of gratitude and thanks. The silver cord
is
loosed, the golden bowl is broken, the pitcher is broken at the fountain and
the
wheel is broken at the cistern. The dust has returned to the earth as it was and
the
spirit has returned to God who gave it.
Although we miss them sadly, our sadness is but for a moment as we
rejoice in the thoughtthat they have traveled to that bourne of time and space from
which no traveler returns and are at long last home; our eternal home, prepared
from eternity, for all of those who profess their faith in God and pledge their
allegiance to Him at the great altar of life, with heart, head and hands upon
the
Holy Bible of the Almighty Architect of the Universe.
This year we have recorded the passing of 3,509 of our brethren. They
have included so very many of our friends and loved ones. Some highly
distinguished within our fraternity and some not so well recognized but now, ALL
on equal terms and equal recognition before God's throne of Grace.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF THE
COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
In accordance with Section 6060 of the California Masonic Code and in
long standing Masonic tradition the Grand Lodge Committee on
with
keeping
Public Schools had endeavored to continue development and promotion of
programs designed to stimulate pride in and support for our California Public
Schools. This has been done in concert with and as a part of the California
Masonic Foundation.
Administrative Set-up

This year two coordinators were chosen by the committee chairman to
assist in the administration of the Public Schools Committee work. Brother Kurt
Knobelauch has ably coordinated the committee'sactivities in the North from San
Luis Obispo to the Oregon border and Brother Albert Wheeler has done yeoman
work coordinating activities in the South from Santa Maria and Bakersfield to the
southern border. Both have reported directly to the Chairman. This has worked
very well. However, it should be noted that there are still some areas in both
Northern and Southern California that are not being adequately covered by
committeemen, and it is resolved that we shall concentrate on resolving this
problem in 1998.

349

Packets

As the beginning of the new Masonic year occurs with the closure of the
Grand Lodge Annual Communication in October it is importnat that the new
Senior Wardens of California Lodges be duly apprised of their responsibilitieswith
respect to Public Schools Month in April. A packet of appropriate sample
materials is compiled and inserted into a large manila envelope or "packet" which
should be helpful by showing him what is available and how to proceed in doing
some of the things that must be done in order to have a successful Public Schools
Month program.
Included in the packet is an attractive pencil imprinted with the Masonic
square and compass and the logo "Freemasons Support Public Schools'', a sample
poster, a Certificate of Appreciation, a Little Red School House Pin, a copy of the
Public Schools Guidelines, a supply order form, a copy of an informative leaflet
which may be ordered free of charge in quantity and a copy of Ten Helpful
Suggestions for Open House Programs at Schools. These packets are included
with other pertinent material from the Communication in a 9"x12" box. It is
important that every Senior Warden or his representative secure this box from the
area designated as the "Mailbox". The Mailbox is located near the Registration
Desk.
Public Schools Month

Meetings

Public Scllools Week has long been a mainstay of the Grand Lodge Public
Schools' annual effort to promote interest in and support for the Public Schools of
California. However, in recent years Grand Masters have chosen to lengthen the
time period for special public schools recognition and have issued their annual
Proclamation as Public Schools Month rather than Public Schools Week.

There have been two regional meetings of the Public Schools Committee
in the South in 1997 and one in the North. These are in addition to the general
meeting of both north and south members which is held at Grand Lodge during the
Annual Communication in October. The committee chairman presides over this
state-wide meeting.

Public Schools committeemen throughout the state have encouraged the
Lodges to actively participate in Public Schools Month observance by participating
in worthwhile programs which will involve the public as well as the schools. Each
committeeman has stood ready, willing and able, if called upon, to assist with ideas
helpful to the development of these programs for the month of April.

These conferences are of considerable importance for the committeemen
for by attending them they are enabled to ascertain recommended procedures,
review available materials, air their concerns, make recommendations and become
acquainted with their counterparts from other sectors of the state and what they are
doing. Thus the committee, as a whole, derives a greater sense of cohesiveness and
espirit de corps.

At the same time it is recognized that our Public Schools need year-round
Lodge and public support and the committeemen work diligently to encourage this
through promotion of the Masonic Student Assistance Program, encouragement of
attendance at school board meetings, volunteerism for school programs, etc.

350

Masonic Student Assistance Program (MSAP)
The Masonic Student Assistance Program has, since 1995, become an
important integral part of the overall effort of the Public Schools Committee to be
ofsignificantassistanceto the children at risk in the Public Schools of California.
Borrowed from a like program which has been in existence for several years in the
state of Pennsylvania two master teachers, Larry Newman and Thom Stecher
conduct nine three-day seminars per year at the Masonic Home in Southern
California.
In essence, this valuable program accepts teachers from all parts of
California, provides them with free transporation, food and lodging at the Masonic
Home in We~t Covina and involves them in a concentrated three-day training
program teach mg them the techniques ofrecognizing children who are at risk from
the nu~e~~us risk ~actors which impinge on the lives of children and how to help
them ut1hzmg services that are offered by various health services availabe through
the schools and through community agencies. The confidential files of identified
children follows throughouttheir school careers and help continues to be afforded
them as they advance through the grades.
To date, hundreds of enthusiastic teachers have been trained in the
professional techniques espoused in these three-day seminars. All costs of the
program, food, lodging and transportation, are absorbedd by the California
Mas~nic Foundation which raises the necessary funds primarily through donations
received from the return address labels that are sent to all California Masonic
families periodically.

Little Red School House Pins
In 1986, Little Red School House Pins first made their appearance as a
~art of the Public Schools Committee program in California to help boost interest
m and support for the public schools of California. They have proven to be a
popular item, particularly among teachers. Hundreds are given away each year to
school personnel who wear them with pride. Some school districts and some
Lo~ges ~rder them in quantity for their teachers and other interested people at the
basic price of$ l .25 each. Otherwise they are used as a give-away item at school
programs, at Teacher of the Year programs, etc.

Teacher of the Year Program
Each year five teachers who have been chosen by their peers from
throughout the state of California are honored at the office of the State School
Board office in Sacramento. The Grand Master, together with the California State

351

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Board Chairman and the State Superintendent of Public Instruation, Delaine
Easton, present these five chosen teachers with a check for $1,000. This money
is to be used to in some way improve the school facilities of the teachers who are
honored. This check, presented by the Grand Master together with a beautifully
framed certificate of recognition really makes the teachers and others who are
present for the ceremony sit up and take notice of the fact that the Masons of
California are really supportive of the public schools as perhaps the most important
institutions in the land.
This year's outstanding teachers awards are presented to Michael Aiello,
San Luis Obispo High School, San Luis Coastal United School District; Stephen
Bock, Woodrow Wilson Elementary School, Selma Unified School District; Carole
Firestone, Lindero Canyon Middle School, Las Virgenes Unified School District,
Agoura Hills; Ralphene Lee Trajan Elementary School, San Juan Unified School
District, Orangeville; and Toni Robinette, Vista Campagna Middle School, Apple
Valley Unified School District.

The Public Schools Newsletter
For the past several years Brother Raymond Young has faithfully edited
quarterly the Public Schools Information Bulletin. This valuable publication has
highlighted many of the important issues which confront our state legislators
regarding our California Public Schools. Eighteen issues have been printed as of
this writing, each of which consists of approximately 14 pages of information of
which the Public Schools committeemen should be apprised. We are most
appreciative of the time and effort our brother has devoted in the compilation of
these valuable information bulletins. This has been truly appreciated, and we thank
him sincerely.

REPORT OF THE COMMIT TEE ON
TEMPLE PROPER TIES AND TAXATI ON

Your Committee on Temple Properties and Taxation has continued to
emphasize that the committee is constituted to assist Temple Associations and
Lodges in operating their real estate through its diverse specialized committee
members. Your committee offers help in the areas of real property management,
purchases and sales, construction, contract negotiation, taxation and relations
between the officers of Temple Associations and Lodges with the aid of members
who are familiar with, and in many instances specialize in, these areas in their daily
vocations. Your committee stresses the importance of conscientious management
of properties while recognizing that local Temple Associations and Lodges are
responsible for, and most capable of, the management of their real property.
Since the members of the committee are spread throughout the state, they
are able to deal with local problems or call on other committee members from other
locales for specific knowledge required to recommend a solution to a local issue.
It is the concerted effort of all members of the committee to suggest or recommend,
rather than dictate, possible solutions to issues brought to their attention.
This year, like many in the recent past, has been an active one for the
committee with many questions being asked by individual Lodges and Temple
Assoications and analyzed and answered by its committee members throughoutthe
state. Specifically, the tax consequences and treatment of the proceeds of the sale
of temple sites have been reviewed and communicated to a number of Lodges and
Temple Associations. Assistance was offered in the documenting the legal status
of Lodges and Temple Associations and clarifying the interactive roles of Lodges
and Temple Associations.
The committee, through its chairman, has participated in two Inspector
meetings and two Lodge officers and temple property officers meetings in
Northern and Southern California by making presentations and answering
questions from the floor in each meeting; it was actively present at one of the two
scheduled workshops for Officer's Management.
During the year, the committee received nine requests for approval of
purchase, sale or renovation of temple sites throughout the state, in execess of
$50,000 each, which were analyzed and reviewed for decision by the Executive
Committee of the Grand Lodge. In accordance with the regulations established by
the Grand Lodge, when requests were received for approval of renovation of
temple sites which were less than $50,000 in total expenditure, these requests were
dealt with by the chairman of the committee without reference to the Executive
Committee.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
TOURNAMENT OF ROSES PARADE FLOAT

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M of California:
Your Committee is charged with the responsibility of arranging all of the
necessary details associated with entering a Masonic Float in the Pasadena Rose
Parade on New Year's Day each year. The purpose of entering a float in this
Parade is summarized briefly as follows:
I.

355

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Freemasonry is presented to the public in a positive manner by displaying
some of our principles and accomplishments, especially our concern for
children and our charitable support in the community. We hope that this
exposure will offset the negative perceptions of Freemasonry
promulgated by our critics and adversaries.

2.

The anniversaries of the various Masonic organizations provide
opportunities to demonstrate to the public that these groups have long
been a part of the Family of Freemasonry, working together for the
benefit of the community.

3.

The float provides an exciting opportunity for our young people to be
involved in an outstanding project.

4.

The float videos which record the entire process of putting a float in the
Parade also provide some information about the fraternity which is
helpful in explaining Freemasonry to non-Masons.

The scope of the Committee's tasks includes the selection of the float
theme, design of the float, contract negotiations with the float builder, fund raising
from members of the Masonic fraternity on a voluntary basis, liaison with the

The theme of the 1997 Rose Parade was "LIFE'S SHINING
MOMENTS". The 1997 Parade coincided with the 75th anniversary of the
International Order of Rainbow for Girls. It was only natural that we should honor
the Rainbow girls on this float and make use of their symbol in the conceptual
design of the float. The float builder, Phoenix Decorating Co. of Pasadena, agreed
with our conceptual design and prepared a rendering of the float for our approval.
We selected the float title "FOLLOW YOUR RAINBOW'' to encourage the
millions of spectators to reach for their pot of gold. We were also made aware that
the Order of the Amaranth would be celebrating its I OOth anniversary in 1997.
The design of the float consisted of a large rainbow emanating from storm
clouds at the rear and terminating in a pot of gold at the front of the float.
Lightning, thunder and simulated rain drops were also represented in the storm
area. In keeping with the Parade theme, several major shining moments were
portrayed in the float design:
a.

The rainbow appearing after the storm represented a shining
moment of nature.

b.

The pot of gold represented a goal in everybody's life.

c.

The seven Rainbow girls riding on the float were Grand Worthy
Advisors in seven jurisdictions throughout North America, the
highest positions which can be attained in the organization.
Both experiences were shining moments in their lives.

d.

A young recipient of a scholarship from the Order of the
Amaranth, dressed in academic cap and gown represented the
moment of graduation from college. Both accomplishments are
shining moments in life.

Selection of the riders on the float was left to the organizations whose
anniversaries were being honored. The Supreme Assembly of the Rainbow for
Girls selected the following Grand Worthy Advisors, each being dressed in a
formal gown in one of the seven colors of the rainbow.

The young lady representing the graduate was Miss Mimi Hoang, a
student at the University of California, San Francisco. She was selected by the
California Masonic Foundation which administers the Amaranth scholarship funds.
All of these young ladies provided a beautiful and colorful addition to the float and
were outstanding ambassadors for their organizations and for Freemasonry
generally.
The television coverage of the 1997 float was fairly good, with time-oncamera ranging from 50 seconds to 1 minute 20 seconds, although some
commentators were silent for many seconds. Unfortunately, our position in the
Parade (unit 91 of 113) was not in our favor because some national networks left
the Parade to cover football games in other parts of the country before the Parade
had completely passed the TV cameras. A 15-minute delay due to a float
breakdown occurred just before our float reached the camera locations.
The cost of the 1997 float was approximately $85,000. Of this amount,
$70,000 was the contracted price of the float and the remainder of the expenses
were for publicity, fund raising, food for the nearly 800 decorators,
correspondence, postage, telephone, photography and videography and other
miscellaneousexpenses. The Committee receives no Grand Lodge appropriation
for its work and Committee members absorb most of their out-of-pocket expenses
to attend meetings and perform their various tasks.
Fund raising for this program continues to be a problem as voluntary
contributions from Grand Lodges, Constituent Lodges, other organizations and
individuals have been steadily declining each year. Fearing that the 1997 float
may be in financialjeopardy, the Float Committee introduced Resolution 95-18 at
the 1995 Annual Communication requesting approval of an assessment of $1 per
person for the 1996-1997 per capita year to support the Rainbow float. This
Resolution failed by only 15 votes and left an unfavorable impression on many
members and the youth groups. Several attempts have been made over the last few

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

357

years to establish a Float Trust Fund with a one dollar contribution from each of
the 250,000 Masons in North America. This would be a one-time-only
contribution which would enable a float to be funded each year from the interest
earned by the Fund without ever asking for another cent. So far, this proposal has
not been supported by the 60 Grand Lodges which comprise the Conference of
Grand Masters.
Fortunately, Grand Master Charles H. Alexander offered his support
through the adoption of a Grand Master's gift pin program proposed by Affinity
Marketing Associates. This program was very successful and enabled the Float
Committee to fulfill its financial obligations for the 1996 float by drawing on some
of these funds. Grand Master Allen B. Gresham continued the pin program du ring
his term as Grand Master and thus ensured that the Rainbow girls would not be
disappointed. We are especially grateful to Grand Master Alexander and Grand
Master Gresham for their vision and assistance in our hour of need.
The Supreme Assembly of the International Order of Rainbow for Girls
was also determined that there would be a Rose Parade float to honor their 75th
anniversary. They organized an anniversary pin sale among their members and
raised more than enough funds to be able to present the Float Committee with a
check for $30,000 toward the float during the public opening of the Grand Lodge
of California in October, 1996.
In addition, the California Rainbow Girls
contributed another $5,500. Taken together, the Rainbow girls financed more
than half of the co~t of the float contract.
The Float Committee has produced a video of each year's float, including
the design, construction and decorating of the float and the television coverage
during the Parade. In addition to providing a record of each float for historical
purposes, these videos serve as useful tools for informing friends and the general
public about various aspects of the Family of Freemasonry. We also furnish a
complimentary copy of each video to every Grand Lodge in North America for use
in their jurisdictions.
The Committee wishes to thank the Trustees of the Masonic Homes of
California for permission to house the visiting Rainbow girls who were riders on
the float, their chaperones and Supreme Assembly leaders at the Covina Home for
the several days that they were in California. This generous hospitality made a
very profound and favorable impression on the visitors. They were most
impressed with the facilities and staff at Covina. The Home and several Float
Committeemen also provided transportation for the visitors to and from the
airports.
Again, the Committee gratefully acknowledges the contributions of many
individuals and organizations in the success of the program. In addition to the

This will be the lead-in to examples such as the Shriners' Hospitals, Masonic
Homes for children, various health clinics, scholarships for children and the
Masonic Model Student Assistance program.
The Float Committee is convinced that the continual presence of the
Family of Freemasonry in the Rose Parade is the most cost-effectiveway to inform
the public about Freemasonry. It is the only Masonic public relations program in
existence which reaches a potential audience of almost half a billion people in more
than 90 countries throughout the world. While we hope to increase the awareness
of the fraternity and its good works, we also recognize that the float program is
only one part of a series of efforts needed to attract high quality members in the
future. We hope that our efforts meet with your approval. We are always
receptive to suggestions for improving our performance and enhancing the image
of the fraternity in the community.

Our special thanks are also extended to Grand Master Gresham, Grand
Lodge officers and the members of the California Masonic Family Forum for their
support and encouragement in this very important program of public relations. We
also appreciate the periodic assistance of the Grand Lodge office staff.

We are now approaching the 1998 New Year's Day Parade and we have
again entered a float. Our 1998 float has been built and is ready to receive its floral
covering. The theme of the 1998 Parade is "HAV'N FUN". Once again, we have
several anniversaries to be recognized. They include the lOOth anniversary of the
Masonic Homes of California, the 75th anniversary of the Shriners' Hospitals and
the 125th anniversary of the Order of Eastern Star. Mention of these anniversaries
and the role of the Family of Freemasonry in the care and support of children will
be included in the script provided to the television stations.
After several meetings to select a float design, we accepted a design
proposed by the float builder, Phoenix Decorating Co., based on the nursery rhyme
about "THE OLD WOMAN WHO LIVED IN THE SHOE". Following the
advice of the float builder, the 1998 float is designed to attract attention and
provide a humorous touch. The shoe is mounted on roller blades and is traveling
down the road to Pasadena when it encounters a scared skunk on the road and
attempts to come to a screeching halt. Riders on the float will include l 0 children
(eight from the Masonic Home at Covina and the Committee Chairman's two
granddaughters),an"old woman" who will be "driving" the rolling shoe and a 99year old resident of the Covina Home for Adults, Dolly Burke, who will celebrate
her lOOth birthday in 1998. In the words of the nursery rhyme, the Old Woman
"had so many children she didn't know what to do, so she fed them some broth
without any bread, then whipped them all soundly and put them to bed". Out TV
script will point out that Masons know what to do - treat them with loving care.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON TRIAL REVIEW
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
Since the 1996 Annual Communication there have been referred to your
Committee on Trial Review ten completed trials. In addition one retrial, pending
since 1993, has become moot. You will hear more of that later. Our log shows the
ten completed trials, one incomplete retrial, now moot, and seven matters pending
but not completed.

361

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

. GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Your committee has reviewed each of the Trial Records numbered 2394,
2395, 2396, 2397, 2399, 2400, 2401, 2402, and 2403 and finds that in each case
there was substantial compliance with the procedural requirements of our
Constitution and Ordinances, and the result is supported by the evidence in the
record of each case and that there are no miscarriages of justice.

For reasons which are not clear, but which should never be repeated, the
Lodge which was directed in 1993 to retry the accused did not do so in 1993, or
1994, or 1995. In late 1996, the proceedings were resumed, after another
communication from the Grand Secretary's office. By this time the accusing
Brother was terminally ill and unable to sign documents or testify at a trial. In
early 1997, the accuser died.
One question posed is whether the case was a business dispute not
involving fraud, in which case it was not unmasonic conduct; or if it did involve
falsehood, deceit or fraud, in which case it would have been unmasonic conduct.
That question is now moot.
The other question is how such delay could have occurred. Since the
Grand Secretary'soffice told the Lodge in 1993 that the Grand Lodge had directed
a new trial, and included new forms to commence the process, and wrote again in
1994 and succeeding years, it is difficult not to blame the Lodge. But we are more
concerned about why we at Grand Lodge did not prod the Lodge more forcefully
into action. We believe that we now have a system of log maintenance which will
prevent such a thing from happening again.
As to this case, we ask that the Grand Lodge approve the dropping of the
charges because the evidence of an offense, if there ever was such proof, has
disappeared with the death of the accuser.
We therefore move the adoption of the following resolution:

360

Your committee therefor submits (and moves for adoption) the following
Resolution:
"Resolved, that in each of Trial Records numbered 2394, 2395, 2396,
2397, 2399, 2400, 2401, 2402, and 2403 the judgment and penalty
imposed be and are ratified, affirmed and approved."
We acknowledge the great behind-the-scenes service·rendered to Lodges
and this Grand Lodge by those Brothers who give of their time and talent to serve
as Trial Masters. We are also grateful to the Grand Secretary's office and
particulary to Brother Joel Springer for their support.
In the past three years we have completed the Manual for Masonic Trials,
supplemented it this year with "A Primer for Those Who Must Prefer Masonic
Charges" helping to eliminate the need for revision before trial of charges made.
We do assist those who bring charges by noting where changes might properly be
made.
No Lodge likes to go through the process of a Masonic trial, but a dozen
times each year some Lodge in this jurisdiction finds itself involved in the process.
If it should come to your Lodge, please familiarize yourself with what is required
so that, if possible, it need not be done twice. We are here to help as well as
review.

Trial Record No. 2347
In 1991, a Master Mason accused a Brother Mason, who was his
employer, of unmasonic conduct. The accusation was that the employer
improperly shunted onto his employee responsibility for a civil lawsuit which
resulted in a default judgment being taken against the accuser for one million
dollars. The accuser said this was after his employer told him that the matter had
been taken care of. At the resulting Masonic trial, the Trial Master ruled that the
evidence of unmasonic conduct was not sufficient to convict and directed the
Commission to enter a Not Guilty verdict. This Grand Lodge, in 1993, reversed
the decision of the Trial Master under the law as it then existed, and ordered that
a new trial of the charges take place.

"Resolved, that Trial Record 2347 be closed without a retrial."

Trial Record No. 2388
In Trial Record No. 2388, a member of Home Lodge No. 721 was
charged in United States District Court with I) securities fraud, and 2) perjury . He
pleaded Guilty to and was found Guilty of each count.
Masonic charges were filed. They alleged the same offenses as had been
charged in federal court. Upon being served with the charges, the accused again
pleaded Guilty to each of the two charges. The Trial Master investigated and
found him Guilty of each count. He then fixed the penalty at Reprimand in Open
Lodge.
The problem in this case is the penalty. The charge of"insider trading"
may be somewhat technical and if that were the only charge the penalty of
Reprimand in Open Lodge might be sufficient. However, the charge of perjury,
in this case lying under oath to the Securities and Exchange Commission, is a
serious Masonic offense. Your committee believes the next higher penalty,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOR NIA

PROCEED INGS OF THE

362

Suspension, is the appropriate penalty. The accused can apply for Restoration
an appropriate time pursuant to Masonic law.
Your committee therefore submits the following Resolution:

at

"Resolved, that in Trial Record No. 2388, the findings of the Trial Master
be affirmed and approved, except that the penalty is raised to Suspension.
Respectfully submitted,
Donald R. Fretz, Chairman

The Junior Wardens Retreats were under the direction of our Senior
Grand Warden, Melville H. Nahin and his wife Alice. These Retreats were built
around Brother Nahin's theme, " THE BEST OF TIMES IS NOW - WHAT A
WONDERFUL WORLD". Subjects covered in these Retreats included, "In Search
of Excellence", "Discovering the Future", "Communication", "Planning Your Year
as Master", "Developing a Lodge Budget", "Reviewing the Books of a Lodge",
"Publicity and Public Relations", "Grand Lodge lnfonnation Sources", "California
Masonic Code", "Passion forthe Membership", "Community Involvement", "The
Secretary as Master's Support", "Friend To Friend", and "The Gift". The ladies
participated in many of the above subjects with their husbands and also covered in
their own sessions subjects on, "Grand Lodge Events", "Planning a Good Event",
"Organization of the Grand Lodge of California", "Masonic Charities", "Ideas for
Community Involvement", "Senior Grand Warden's Remarks", and "Freemasonry:
Today-Tomorrow-2000". This training was also reinforced with Team Building
Exercises and Group Reports. The Junior Wardens and their ladies left these
Retreats with a better understanding of Freemasonry, their leadership role in the
Lodge and how to make their Lodges successful.
Speakers used in these sessions included Anthony P. Wordlow, Melville
H. Nahin, Alvin J. Weis, Stanley M. Cazneaux, John L. Cooper, Fred Kleyn, Fred
Sorsabal, Loyal Stark and Robert Winterton. A special thank you to Robert
Winterton who has spoken at every session over the past nine years. He is an
exceptional speaker with the ability to mix good humor with a hard-hitting
message. In addition, Mark Gibson, James H. Leach, David Decker, Julius Kahn
Ill, Sam Levin, David Doan and Kelly Wiest were also guest speakers, and did and
outstanding job. The ladies speakers included Marilyn Wordlow, Alice Nahin,
Virginia Weis, Gloria Cazneaux Marlene Sorsabal, and Nancy Decker. I want to
thank each of these ladies for their participation and for an excellent job.
A very special thank you is extended to Kimberly Hegg of the Grand
Lodge office staff for the outstanding support she has provided. She always
provides quality material in a very professional manner for the Retreats.
For myself, I want to once again express my deep appreciation to the
Grand Lodge Officers for their continuing support of the Wardens Retreats and to
the members of the Committee for their dedication to this important Program. Once
again, I extend to my wife Gloria, a very special thank you for without her
